text:
A rush transcript of "This Week with George Stephanopoulos" airing on Sunday, July 19, 2026 on ABC News is below. This copy may not be in its final form, may be updated and may contain minor transcription errors. For previous show transcripts, visit the "This Week" transcript archive.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

JONATHAN KARL, ABC “THIS WEEK” CO-ANCHOR: Breaking news overnight. The war in Iran takes a dark turn, with the first U.S. combat deaths in four months. “THIS WEEK” starts right now.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: Major escalation. Stunning video circulating online appears to show the strikes that killed two American service members in Jordan, with another still missing. And as the conflict escalates in the Middle East, concern about rising energy prices here at home. When will it end? How will Trump retaliate? His energy secretary joins us live.

The 2020 election obsession.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: If there can be no trust, there can be no greatness.

KARL: Even some Republicans are saying it’s time for Trump to move on.

SEN. JOHN CORNYN (R) TEXAS: We have 109 days until the midterm elections, and I don’t understand talking about what happened six years ago.

SEN. BILL CASSIDY, (R) LOUISIANA: We should be talking about what matters to the people around the kitchen table.

KARL: We’ll talk to Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee.

And a comedy star wins a big honor.

It seems like it’s like the Nobel Prize for comedy.

BILL MAHER, COMEDIAN & 2026 MARK TWAIN PRIZE RECIPIENT: There’s not many for this particular brand of show business. So, I was very grateful.

KARL: We’ll go inside Bill Maher’s podcast studio to talk to him about his relationship with President Trump and the state of American politics.

Could you see yourself voting for J.D. Vance?

MAHER: Yes. If this is the Democratic side, yes.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

ANNOUNCER: From ABC News, it’s "This Week." Here now, Jonathan Karl.

KARL: Good morning. Welcome to this week.

We want to get right to that sad news out of the Middle East. The first American combat deaths since the opening days of the war more than four months ago. Two U.S. service members were killed at a base in Jordan. Another one is missing. And several more were injured. Overnight, U.S. forces responded with another round of airstrikes on Iran.

So, let’s get right to senior White House correspondent Rachel Scott.

Rachel, what are you learning this morning?

RACHEL SCOTT, SENIOR WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT: Yes, Jon. Well, this is the first time that U.S. soldiers have been killed in this conflict since that agreement between the U.S. and Iran fell apart weeks ago. We're learning this morning that those two U.S. service members were killed after Iran bombarded a military base in Jordan, where U.S. forces had been stationed. And as you mentioned, one remains missing at this hour.

This video circulating from the base on the day of that attack. Four other service members were injured and taken to hospitals in Jordan. They have since been discharged. So far, 16 American troops have died in this war with Iran, 427 U.S. troops have been wounded so far.

The president, just weeks ago, was optimistic about an end to the war. But the U.S. struck Iran once again overnight. And he said just a few days ago, Iran wanted to make a deal. But it is clear, these diplomatic talks have severely stalled. And now 140 days into this war, there’s no end in sight.

KARL: The video of that attack is alarming. How is the president reacting?

SCOTT: Well, President Trump called the deaths a shame. He called it very sad. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the loss of U.S. soldiers only stiffens our resolve.

But the question now for the president is, how much does this change the strategy ahead, especially after he promised this conflict would be brief? He campaigned on keeping America out of foreign wars. But does this lead now to a much wider conflict, Jon?

KARL: All right, our thanks to Rachel.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright joins us now.

Secretary Wright, thank you for being here.

We saw U.S. forces struck Iran for the eighth night in a row last night. Is the president planning any further retaliation for the killing of those two U.S. service members?

CHRIS WRIGHT, ENERGY SECRETARY: Yes, look, the president’s mission is essential for peace in the Middle East and peace in the world. And that is to prevent Iran from achieving nuclear weapons and to degrade their ability to terrorize their neighbors and the world and global commerce. So, yes, this mission will go on until the mission is done.

KARL: But I’m asking you, does he plan retaliation for the killing of those U.S. service members?

WRIGHT: It’s tragic to lose American lives, but this is a mission that will save countless lives going forward. His focus is on degrading the Iranian ability to terrorize the world, to hold world commerce hostage, as they are doing right now, and to prevent Iran from getting nuclear weapons. That is unchanged.

KARL: You were on this show back in March. And I want to play a -- something of what you said about how long this war would last.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

WRIGHT (March 15, 2026): I think that this conflict will certainly come to the end in the next few weeks. Could be sooner than that.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: So, you said it would certainly come to an end within a few weeks. We are now nearly five months into this war. How does it end? When does it end?

WRIGHT: Well, the plan -- we needed four to six weeks for military actions. They went for five and a half weeks. We did a pause to try to get an agreement with the Iranian people to allow oil to flow without them attacking it. They’ve proven unwilling to do that. And we’ve pivoted.

Now what we’re doing is assuring that -- that oil and gas and other products can flow through the Strait of Hormuz, with or without Iranian cooperation. And we’ve continued to degrade their offensive military capabilities. The president is always looking for the diplomatic off ramp. President Trump wants to end it with a peaceful agreement with Iran, but it takes two parties to do that. If they’re -- if they’re -- if they’re ready to do that, that’s the way it will end. If not, we will continue to assure flow of traffic through the Strait without Iran’s cooperation.

KARL: But we’re not seeing flow now, right? I mean, hasn’t flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz effectively stopped over the past few days?

WRIGHT: Oh, absolutely not. Absolutely not. I get the data on that every day. The seven-day trailing average right now is just under seven million barrels a day flowing through the waterway and just under seven million barrels a day additional flow through the bypass pipelines. So, we’re at a little under 14 million barrels a day from the Arabian Gulf region. That’s two-thirds of pre-conflict traffic, dramatically up from where we were back in March when I was last on your show.

KARL: I mean --

WRIGHT: Not 100 percent yet, but two-thirds of flow right now.

KARL: And that’s over the past few days. When’s that average? We saw the numbers from Thursday were simply eight ships going through the Strait of Hormuz. That’s far below.

WRIGHT: So, almost all the public -- almost all the public data I’ve seen is incorrect. There’s flow through two routes through the Strait of Hormuz. There’s up near the Iranian islands that’s flow complicit with Iran, but that’s not nothing. And then there’s flow through the southern route that’s protected by American infrastructure. And we count the volume of oil that goes through. The ship numbers are down more dramatically. But, of course, we’re flowing larger tankers now to keep the world markets as well supplied as we can.

Gasoline prices today are more than one dollar a gallon cheaper than they were four years ago under the Biden administration. And we’ll do everything we can to drive them further down in the weeks and months ahead.

KARL: And we’ve seen over the -- over the past week the price of oil go up, the price of gas go up. The Iranian IRGC is now saying that if the U.S. strikes continue, they will go to what they are calling full scale assault and annihilation and try to smash infrastructure, specifically energy infrastructure, in the region. What are they capable of doing, and what are the implications for the price of oil and the price of gas?

WRIGHT: Well, clearly, as we’ve seen, decades of focusing their entire economy on armament has made a very prickly Iran. They’ve continued to attack their neighbors, shamelessly civilian targets, at least as much as military targets. We don’t have any reason to believe they will stop that, but we are continuing to shrink their ability to execute those attacks. And we are doing this in coordination and in partnership with all their neighbor countries that they are assaulting.

KARL: OK. Mr. Secretary, while I’ve got you here, a different topic. The president made it clear this week that he views election security as a top domestic priority, yet we saw his budget has cut CISA, the cybersecurity agency, by $700 million. If he’s so concerned about possible foreign interference in our elections, why does his budget cut the agency that would be charged with preventing that?

WRIGHT: Well, look, there’s many cybersecurity agencies across the government. We meet regularly on that topic, and our efforts have done nothing but ramp up. Sure, they’ve gotten more sophisticated and a different focus of them, but I wouldn’t look at the inputs, the money spent. I’d look at the outputs, the quality of United States cybersecurity. That’s never been higher than where it is right now under President Trump.

KARL: Never been higher. And you’re including election security in that?

WRIGHT: Across the board, we are looking at cybersecurity from threats from adversaries. I've not been involved in the election efforts, so I can't comment on them. But obviously, having trust in American systems of government and keeping our nation secure is top priority for the Trump administration.

KARL: And one last question before you go, really simple one. Did Joe Biden win the 2020 presidential election?

WRIGHT: He was president for four years. Clearly so.

KARL: He clearly won the election.

WRIGHT: Look, I'm not an election evaluator, but it sure seems to me like he did.

KARL: Okay. Secretary Wright, thank you very much. Appreciate it.

WRIGHT: Thank you.

KARL: As the war with Iran escalated this week, President Trump chose to address the nation Thursday night in primetime on an entirely different subject. He issued an alarming warning about what he called the, quote, “shocking” vulnerabilities in our election systems.

He zeroed in, in particular, on the one presidential election that he lost, 2020, and he declassified a trove of intelligence documents he claimed proved that foreign powers, particularly China, had meddled in that election.

Much has already been said by intelligence experts and by prominent figures in both parties about how the president made unfounded and reckless allegations without evidence, and about how the documents he released revealed little new information about election vulnerabilities.

So let me take a moment instead to point out some of what those documents actually did reveal. For one, even as President Trump tried to alarm the country about foreign interference and the way we count our votes, the documents released showed very nearly the opposite. One of them, an intelligence assessment issued while he was president in January of 2020, says America's election system, quote, “would be difficult to manipulate on a wide enough scale to alter the election outcome”.

And while he warned again and again about China, the documents that he himself declassified showed that the only country actually observed attempting to target, access, or manipulate election-related systems was Russia, a country he referred to only in passing in his roughly 25-minute speech.

As for China, he told us it had pulled off, in his words, the largest compromise of election data in history, the illicit acquisition of 220 million American voter files, which he called an unprecedented election security nightmare.

But buried in the very documents that President Trump released is the fact that the information was, quote, “publicly available for download from commercial websites”. It doesn't need to be hacked or stolen. It's data that can be legally bought, the kind of -- the kind that political campaigns purchase all the time.

And the Chinese obtained that data in 2022, after the election, the president claims, was rigged.

But the single most significant thing to me in all of these documents that the president declassified Thursday night was this: an intelligence assessment warning that one of the most damaging things that a foreign power could do is not to hack a voting machine, but to convince Americans that they had done that.

As one of the documents Trump declassified warned, quote, “Adversaries could make wholly fabricated claims that they have compromised all U.S. voting machines. And those claims could introduce public doubts about the validity of the election and undercut public confidence in the election.”

Think about that. The intelligence community, in the very documents that Trump himself declassified, assessed that one of the most damaging things a foreign adversary could do would be to falsely convince the American people that their elections had been rigged.

And here's the irony. The person who has attempted to do exactly that over and over again for nearly six years, and most dramatically on Thursday night, is Donald Trump, who, against the very evidence that he himself presented, tried to tell millions of Americans that foreign powers had corrupted an election, specifically the one election he lost.

And I'm joined now by Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee.

So I want to get to all of that with you, but first, the situation in Iran. We've seen two American service members killed by Iranian missile, presumably.

What should the president do to respond to that?

SEN. MARK WARNER, (D) VIRGINIA & INTELLIGENCE COMMITTEE VICE CHAIR: Well, first of all, I join with all Americans in condolences to these soldiers. Remember, as we think about this five-month war, this is a war of choice. As a member of the Gang of Eight, there was no imminent threat from Iran against America. So, Donald Trump chose to go to war. It took him two weeks to lay out what he thought his goals were going to be.

Let’s go through those. Regime change. How we doing there? We got a worse crowd than before. Getting the enriched uranium. Well, it’s still there. As a matter of fact, it would take a minimum of 15,000 troops on the ground for a week to try to take these canisters, which are quite volatile, out of the -- their bunkers. Getting rid of Iran’s missile and drone capability. Obviously, we’ve not been successful there. And the thing, Jon, that makes me completely crazy is, Iran has both missiles, and they also have lots and lots of $50,000 drones that are very effective.

We are using missiles that cost $2.5 million to shoot down those drone -- those drones. President Zelenskyy, the only country that has devised a technique of counter Iranian drones at $5,000. They’ve done it so effectively. They offered us all of that technology for free. And the Trump White House basically said to the Ukrainians, thanks, but no thanks. So, we are behind on that as well.

And then finally, on the Strait of Hormuz, I mean, I don’t -- I don’t know what gas station the secretary’s going to, but before the war, average price of gasoline in Virginia was $2.81. It is now back to $4. Diesel’s at $5. You know, I see no path in the short term how the Strait is going to be settled. This war of choice has been a disaster. It has been a disaster militarily. It has been a disaster in terms of how we’re viewed around the world. It has been a disaster to our friends and allies who have questioned whether we will keep our promises. I’m anxious if it takes a classic Donald Trump move, declare victory tomorrow and be done. But the continuation of this war at this pace will be a continuing disaster.

KARL: But you have a situation where the Iranians are firing missiles at ships going through the Strait. They’re attacking U.S. bases in the region. I mean, the United States could walk away. The president could declare victory and leave. But the Iranian -- how do you stop what the Iranians are doing?

WARNER: Well, we --

KARL: I mean, how do you end it?

WARNER: In a normal process, you would have had diplomacy negotiated by diplomats who actually knew what they were doing. There was a reason it took years with people with great expertise to negotiate what now suddenly looks pretty good, what was called the JCPOA, that allowed us to have international versions --

KARL: The Obama nuclear deal, right?

WARNER: That was under Obama. Years to get there. The Iranians, give them credit, they know about enriched uranium. They know about nuclear. They have -- send great negotiators. But we’re not going to -- I do not believe anyone thinks that we’re going to bomb Iran into submission. And I sure as heck do not believe that short of troops on the ground, that there’s any meaningful path to get out that enrichment uranium.

KARL: Do you -- do you agree with your colleague, Senator Ed Markey, who is calling for cutting off all funding to the war? Would that be a mistake? Because then we have troops in the region --

WARNER: We have troops in the region. I would say this, the Defense Department will ask for additional funds. And we are running down some of our supplies. My response to that is, there is $89 billion of money that DOD is sitting on that has not been allocated to specific programs. There are shortages in the region. DOD, use that money first to replenish our supplies. And if the president wants to continue this war, come to Congress, make his case to the American people and to Congress rather than continuing what I think now is, frankly, an illegal action, because he never went through that process.

KARL: Let me turn to the election -- comments the president made about the election security. First of all, you’re on -- you’re on the -- you’re the vice chair of the Intel Committee. Was there anything new in what he released?

WARNER: I’ve been chair or vice chair for the last decade. There’s probably no issue I’ve been more obsessed about going all the way back to the Russia campaign. Russia was very good at influencing our elections. They have been far and away the most prominent player, usually on behalf of Trump. Iran has been very active as well, usually against Trump. North Korea has been active. China’s got the capabilities, but they’ve been more -- less about which candidate and more like, can we just make Americans lose confidence?

KARL: And the 220 million voter files, is there any concern there? I mean, I --

WARNER: Well, listen, I'm much more concerned about the fact that the Chinese hacked into the OPM data a number of years back and got personal information about anybody working on the federal government.

KARL: On government employees. Yes.

WARNER: I'm more concerned about the fact that they tapped into many insurance companies and have got personal information about all of us. They have incredible data capabilities. And again, the secretary, respectfully, our cybersecurity activity is CISA. It has worked with the private sector. He's cut it like mad. We have another part of election security, and remarkably, Jon, a lot of these election security apparatus was set up, done under President Trump's first term. They did a good job.

KARL: Yes.

WARNER: There was something called the Elections Assistance Commission. It is -- nobody knows about it, but it works with local registrars, state registrars, making sure we vet voting machines. Recently, Trump fired all the senior leadership, made the Republican quit, fired the Democrats. You know, this guy is not looking for a secure election because if we have a free and fair election, he and his allies are going to get beat historically this fall.

KARL: Now, I understand that you and I think every other Democrat opposed this so-called SAVE America Act. And there's a lot of reasons that you've put forward. But let me ask you very narrowly on the issue of photo I.D., requiring photo I.D. to register to vote, to vote. Is this something that Democrats should get behind?

WARNER: We have --

KARL: I mean, 80 some percent of Americans, 71 percent of Democrats say they favor this.

WARNER: You know what? In Virginia, we have voter I.D. and photo I.D. I got to show my --

KARL: That's actually not the case. I mean, I'm a Virginia voter. You don't need to show a photo I.D. in Virginia. There are wide range of things you can show for I.D., and if you don't show one of those, you can sign an affidavit saying, attesting --

WARNER: You can sign an affidavit. And those become --

KARL: But it's not required.

WARNER: Those become ballots that if you want to contest later can be contested. But you are have -- you do have a variety of documents, but we have voter I.D. of one form or another.

(CROSSTALK)

KARL: Should that be a national standard, that you have to show an I.D.?

WARNER: Are you -- the irony here would be the case. If you can show any photo that has government stamped, it would be fine. Certain states will say, we're going to let you show your NRA gun license, but you can't show your student I.D.. If you're going to have a set of I.D.s, let's have it across the board as long as it comes from some official point. But this is not about voter I.D..

The SAVE Act is about voter disenfranchisement. The SAVE Act is going to take anybody that changed their name when they got married, they don't get to vote unless they can come back and find the person --

KARL: And if you don't have an I.D., if you don't have your passport. All right.

WARNER: And Jon -- but, Jon, just stay on this for a minute.

KARL: Yes.

WARNER: Lisa Murkowski, a host of Republicans don't want the SAVE Act because they know it's anti-voter.

KARL: All right.

WARNER: But the folks who have mail-in voting, Utah is as Republican a state as anyone. They've done mail-in voting for decades. Donald Trump wants to decrease voter participation.

KARL: So --

WARNER: And undermine confidence in our system.

KARL: We're out of time. Before you go, though, are you going to vote for Jay Clayton to be the director of National Intelligence?

WARNER: I've known Jay for a long time. I like him, but after his performance before my committee, his inability to answer the question about who won the 2020 election or commenting on Gabbard, the previous DNI's effort to interfere in the Fulton County elections, I am not going to vote for him. If we confirm --

KARL: Now, if he doesn't get confirmed, Bill Pulte remains the head of --

(CROSSTALK)

WARNER: And that is a rock and a hard place.

KARL: All right.

WARNER: But I think Jay Clayton will get confirmed. And God willing, I hope the guy that becomes DNI is the guy that I've known and liked and worked with.

KARL: All right, Mark Warner, thank you very much for being here.

Up next, President Trump's teleprompter operator was caught allegedly cashing in on his speeches back in March, but he wasn't taken off the job until ABC News broke the story this week. More on that when we get back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

KARL: Now to the latest on alleged conflicts of interest in the Trump White House. As the President's Truth Social platform is looking to sell early access to his social media posts, and his teleprompter operator allegedly cashes in on his inside knowledge of the president's speeches.

Here's our chief investigative correspondent, Aaron Katersky.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

AARON KATERSKY, ABC NEWS’ CHIEF INVESTIGATIVE CORRESPONDENT (voice-over): A president's words can move markets, and the president is now moving to monetize his words. His financial disclosure released earlier this month showed President Trump, America's dealmaker-in-chief, has already made more than $2 billion since returning to office.

DONALD TRUMP, PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: You know why I'm profiting because the stock market's going up. Everybody's profiting.

KATERSKY (voice-over): This week, he found a path to another potential White House windfall. His social media company said it will begin selling instant access to posts from top accounts on Truth Social, where Trump regularly announces policy moves, military actions, personnel choices, and other consequential decisions.

SEN. ADAM SCHIFF, (D) CALIFORNIA: This is the president saying, give me a cut, and I'll give you the opportunity to make money off my statements, just as I make money off my own statements.

KATERSKY (voice-over): The president's financial advisors have traded stock on his behalf, investing in companies whose share prices are impacted by those social media posts.

TRUMP: I don't get involved in my personal. We have funds that run my money.

KATERSKY (voice-over): During his first year back in the White House, Trump's annual financial report showed his money managers made more than 21,000 securities trades, growing his accounts to more than $850 million, with stakes in 1,600 companies, some of them directly involved in deals tied to his administration.

In this post, he praised Elon Musk and reassured the public that Musk's companies would continue getting large-scale subsidies from the government. At the time, no one knew his investment advisors, one day prior, purchased hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of Tesla stock.

And when Trump posted about the very big and exciting news that computer chipmaker Nvidia would build A.I. supercomputers in the U.S., he did not disclose his advisors had purchased hundreds of thousands of dollars of Nvidia stock days before.

The White House has repeatedly denied financial wrongdoing and says the president only acts in the best interests of the American public.

This week, in a story first reported by ABC News, it was someone working for Trump, allegedly trying to profit from the presidency.

TRUMP: I have a guy, Gabe. He's excellent. I've had some real bad ones, but I have Gabe.

KATERSKY (voice-over): As Trump's teleprompter operator since 2016, Gabriel Perez was the man who knew what Trump would say before he said it. Sources told ABC News he used his inside knowledge to bet on the contents of Trump's speeches, winning tens of thousands of dollars on the prediction market Kalshi.

TRUMP: My fellow Americans. Our nation is back.

KATERSKY (voice-over): Perez was there for the State of the Union.

TRUMP: You know, religion's back now hotter than ever before.

KATERSKY (voice-over): The National Prayer Breakfast.

TRUMP: The USA is the economic engine on the planet.

KATERSKY (voice-over): And the World Economic Forum.

For those speeches and more, the sources said Perez took advantage of his unique insight into Trump's remarks on Kalshi's mentions market, where users bet on whether certain words and phrases will be uttered.

Over a three-month period beginning last December, sources said Perez traded on more than a dozen of the president's speeches and won more than $100,000, sometimes backing out of bets mid-speech if Trump skipped certain words.

TRUMP: You know, when you go up here, you take a big chance, especially me, because I go off teleprompter about 80 percent of the time.

KATERSKY (voice-over): Kalshi said its own surveillance team promptly flagged and referred these trades to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which is responsible for regulating prediction markets.

KATERSKY: What's at stake in this room?

ROBERT DENAULT, KALSHI HEAD OF ENFORCEMENT & LEGAL COUNSEL: The integrity of our markets.

KATERSKY (voice-over): Kalshi prohibits users from trading on confidential information obtained at work, as the company told us back in May when we visited the room where it investigates suspicious trades.

DENAULT: So if you have information by virtue of your job or your employment, something that you have a legal duty surrounding, and you have an obligation not to take that and misappropriate it for yourself.

KATERSKY (voice-over): Sources said Perez made its last trade in March. Later that same month, the White House issued an internal memo warning staff not to use non-public information to place bets on prediction markets.

KAROLINE LEAVITT, WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY: There are very strict ethical guidelines here at the White House that explicitly state not to do this.

KATERSKY (voice-over): Sources said Perez is in talks now with the CFTC to settle the allegations, which could force him to give back the profits from his bets.

The White House said President Trump put Perez on indefinite leave for taking advantage of his position.

LEAVITT: He believes it's deeply unfortunate and frankly, a disgrace.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

KARL: While the White House called the teleprompter operator's alleged actions a disgrace, he was caught back in March and continued to work operating the president's teleprompter until this week, only put on leave after ABC News broke the story.

Coming up, two Republicans who could derail Todd Blanche's nomination for Attorney General. The Roundtable is next.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

KARL: The roundtable is all here.

Former DNC chair Donna Brazile, “NOTUS” political columnist Dana Milbank, “SCOTUSblog” editor Sarah Isgur, and “National Review:” editor Ramesh Ponnuru.

So, Ramesh, President Trump sure seemed like he wanted to end the war with Iran, but the Iranians weren’t going to go along with it.

RAMESH PONNURU, NATIONAL REVIEW EDITOR & ABC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: This administration started this war with a strategy of wishful thinking, and it has turned out to be harder to get out of a war than to get into one. Part of the problem is the bad faith of the Iranian negotiators. But another problem is the gap between the administration’s claims that it won the war and the reality that it didn’t. And it’s hard to bridge that gap in order to bridge the gap between Iran and the U.S. at the same time.

KARL: Yes, it wasn’t long ago -- I think it was about a month ago -- that J.D. Vance, the vice president, was talking about how Iran had turned over a new leaf, I think was the phrase he used.

I want to play something that he said this week to Joe Rogan as part of a three hour interview.

Take a listen to this.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

J.D. VANCE, VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: You have seen this very discreet, extremely well-funded campaign to try to derail the negotiation and try to derail the deal. There are some people within their system, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, who are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: Now, here’s the thing. He wasn’t talking about the Iranians. He was talking about the Israelis.

So, Sarah, the vice president making the case that it was the Israelis that were trying to tank his peace talks. Was it the Israelis or was it the Iranians? What --

SARAH ISGUR, EDITOR AT SCOTUSBLOG & ABC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: This is J.D. Vance’s 2028 campaign finding itself between a rock and a hard place, where J.D. Vance is supposed to be the isolationist, no more wars candidate. He is the vice president for a president who now, quite clearly, started a war of choice and can’t get out of it. And so, J.D. Vance is going to have to come up with what his message is going to be.

I mean, as soon as after the midterms, Donald Trump is now going to be sort of shuffled off to the side as we look at 2028 and who those nominees are going to be. J.D. Vance is in a rough spot.

KARL: Donna.

DONNA BRAZILE, FORMER DNC CHAIR & ABC NEWS CONTRIBUTOR: The political stakes could not be higher. Look, we just lost two more American service members, one missing, and hopefully that service member could be found and alive. This has cost the American people over $1,300 (ph) since the war started. The MOU is less than thirty days old. The administration still has no strategy, no plan. And when they signed the documents, there were so many holes in it, we knew that the Iranians would figure out a way to violate whatever they put in writing. The Strait was never fully reopened. And you have an administration that now, their only strategy is just to keep bombing the hell out of Iran.

When will it end? We don’t know. What’s the strategy? We don’t know.

DANA MILBANK, NOTUS POLITICAL COLUMNIST: The Vance remarks were particularly important, I think, because, I mean, I think what we’re seeing right now is the crackup of the 80-year U.S.-Israel alliance there. We saw it on the left this week.

KARL: Fall apart (ph)?

MILBANK: Half of the Democratic Party in the House voted to cut off military aid to Israel. You had 40 Senate -- Democratic senators earlier on a similar piece of legislation.

But we’re also seeing it, you know, the MAGA coalition, the young evangelical Christians no longer supportive of Israel. So, Bibi Netanyahu, AIPAC made this big bet that this coalition would right (ph). And it seems to have disappeared. Israel has elections October 27th. If Bibi’s returned, I think that’s a -- I think that’s pretty much the end.

PONNURU: And what’s going on in each party is linked in this way. The Republicans can distance themselves from Israel because the Democrats are sprinting away from Israel. So,

if you're a pro-Israel voter and you don't like what Vice President Vance is saying, what's your alternative? A Democratic Party that is moving further and further away.

KARL: I mean, you have Mamdani this week suggesting that he may, in fact, try to arrest Bibi Netanyahu when he shows up in New York for the U.N. General Assembly in September.

And J.D. Vance saying that Epstein, he believes, had connections to senior levels of Mossad, the Israeli intelligence.

ISGUR: And not surprising that we're seeing anti-Semitism rise as well, not just here in the U.S., but globally. These are trends that we are seeing in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis that, again, are not Trump-specific. They are international.

And that is populism on the rise, anger, political violence, and anti-Semitism being a big part of that as well.

KARL: I want to turn to another big thing that happened this week. That was the Todd Blanche confirmation hearing. He was asked a very simple question by a friendly senator that seemed to have a bit of a Freudian slip.

Take a listen.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

SEN. JOHN KENNEDY, (R) LOUISIANA: Are you and President Trump friends?

TODD BLANCHE, ACTING ATTORNEY GENERAL: I'm his lawyer, was his lawyer, and now, I'm the deputy attorney general.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: How did he do, Dana?

MILBANK: I think he was -- he was right the first time.

He didn't do well, but does it matter at all? He is -- he is almost certainly going to be confirmed. We saw Thom Tillis already heading in that direction. John Cornyn certainly, if passed his prologue, will cave on this as well.

KARL: Unclear. Sarah, you have an insight into this. Is Cornyn going to vote against him?

ISGUR: I think he probably will. What's funny is this vote doesn't matter, but that cuts both ways, right? He is the acting attorney general and will remain so, whether he is confirmed or not.

KARL: You mean the overall confirmation vote. If he doesn't get confirmed, he remains acting attorney general.

ISGUR: He's still acting attorney general.

And so on the one hand, John Cornyn voting no would be a big shot over the bow to Donald Trump, but it wouldn't change the facts on the ground at the Department of Justice. Voting yes wouldn't send a message to Donald Trump, but it also won't change the facts on the ground for the Department of Justice.

In the end, I think John Cornyn will decide that this is better than what the alternative could be and probably vote yes.

KARL: And Tillis made him sit down with -- meet with Epstein victims. That didn't seem to go very well.

PONNURU: No, but it seems to me that Senator Tillis was trying to create a test that the nominee could easily pass, which is just have the meeting in the first place.

BRAZILE: I think we should look at his record. I mean, we should look at the way he has conducted himself over the last few months. Being the president, you know, go-to guy for weaponization, for going after the president’s perceived enemies, for the $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund, the IRS settlement.

There's so many things to litigate when it comes to Todd Blanche. I hope the Senate reject this nomination.

KARL: All right. I promised you I was going to show you what the Blue Angels commander said about that flyover that was praised by Secretary Hegseth.

Take a listen.

(BEGIN VIDEO CLIP)

BLUE ANGELS COMMANDING OFFICER: The pilot found himself, unfortunately, in a situation that we would deem unsafe over the beach. We never intend to fly over the crowd that low.

(END VIDEO CLIP)

KARL: He said it was unsafe, said that they would never do it again.

PONNURU: It was below the standards that they have. Look, my uncle --

KARL: But he -- this was praised by the defense secretary.

BRAZILE: Well --

KARL: So who's right, Donna, the commander of the Blue Angels or the defense secretary?

BRAZILE: Look, I love my Uncle Johnny. He's a second generation, second, second generation Tuskegee airman. And whenever I think about the military, especially Air Force, I consult him because he knows he said this is a F/A-18 Super Hornet.

It flew lower than a team standard demonstration, you know, profile. So congratulations on the 80th anniversary to the Blue Angels. But this was a no, no.

MILBANK: Well, Pete Hegseth wants to make sure everybody gets tested for testosterone. But it seems to me the problem may be that he has too much testosterone going on right now.

And that, you know, as you know, a little bit too much of that can --

KARL: I don't know. I mean, I --

(LAUGHTER)

MILBANK: As you personally know, it can make you extra aggressive, and it can blur your vision just a little bit.

It wasn't just him. Hung Cao, the naval secretary, said no reprimand, no firings, no problem.

So it does seem to be this sort of chest-thumping part of the military that we're seeing here.

KARL: By the way, before we were you surprised either one of you about the teleprompter operator?

ISGUR: So I actually think, you know, in that piece by Aaron Katersky, we should separate this into two different buckets. Trump's stock trades and Trump's team's stock trades are grift and would be the biggest news story in America 20 years ago.

The teleprompter thing actually seems more like a story about the potential for these betting markets to have a temptation power over public officials and --

KARL: Across the board.

ISGUR: Across the board. I think this could have happened in any administration and it is something, again, we shouldn't look at as a Trump corruption problem. We should look at it as a, what are we doing about betting --

(CROSSTALK)

BRAZILE: (Inaudible) never ends with this administration.

(LAUGH)

PONNURU: You are the teleprompter operator, this White House. And you're looking at the president enriching himself. I think it would be hard to tell yourself it would be ethically wrong for me to exploit my power and make some money off it. Everybody else around me is.

KARL: DOES it make you wonder how many other federal employees are thinking the same thing? No.

(LAUGH)

BRAZILE: As a former federal employee, I -- this has open up a new chapter on corruption.

(LAUGH)

BRAZILE: It never ends.

KARL: Right.

BRAZILE: I mean, the inside trading. You know, the, I'm going to appear with Tesla guy tomorrow, but today, you know, I'll get a couple of trades in.

MILBANK: But you can picture the guy's thought process, as Ramesh was saying, president made $2 billion last year. I just want $100,000. What's wrong with that?

BRAZILE: Yeah, chump change.

(LAUGH)

BRAZILE: While the American people are suffering.

KARL: Unbelievable. All right. We've got to take a quick break.

Up next, a candid conversation with Bill Maher about his dinner with Trump and who he thinks should win the midterms.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

KARL: Comedian and talk show host, Bill Maher, has shown a willingness to call out hypocrisy on both sides of the aisle. He was recently awarded the nation's highest honor for comedy, the "Mark Twain Prize for American Humor" from the Kennedy Center. I talked with Maher this week at his home in Los Angeles.

KARL: Well, congratulations on winning the Mark Twain Award.

BILL MAHER, COMEDIAN AND TALK SHOW HOST: Thank you.

KARL: It seems like it's like the Nobel Prize for comedy.

MAHER: There aren't a lot of awards for comedy, and it's pretty overlooked, like in movies. But for -- for what I do, it is yes, the award, I think, to get. And again, there's not many for this particular brand of show business, so I was very grateful.

KARL: Now, the White House reaction to the news that you were getting this award was really something.

(LAUGH)

KARL: I mean -- I want to read it exactly. Karoline Leavitt, the Press Secretary, "This is fake news. Bill Maher is not getting this award." Steve Cheung, the Comms Director, "Literally fake news." What was going on with that?

MAHER: I don't know, but it was lovely to see him at the awards.

(LAUGH)

KARL: I mean, it's not the first time --

MAHER: Actually, there were a lot of Trump people at, you know, people in the administration. Pam Bondi came, you know, and I'm glad. But it was not a conservative crowd. It was -- it was a mixed crowd. And they both liked me.

(LAUGH)

MAHER: So to me, that was like, there, boom. That's what I've been doing.

KARL: But what do you think was going on? Because he controlled -- he's the Chairman of the Kennedy Center, it was the board that chose you --

MAHER: He was just mad at me because I went to his house for dinner with no guarantee that I would leave -- guarantee? It was never in the cards that I was ever going to come over to their -- his side. But, you know, it was set up as rather than just screaming at each other, all these insults.

KARL: Yes. Yes.

MAHER: You know, the first thing I did that you saw on the special, the page that he signed with the 56 different things he's called me. I love stuff like that.

KARL: Yes

MAHER: You know, it's better to just talk and go through this. But, you know, I mean, those people, they really have no argument for not doing it.

KARL (voice-over): Maher faced backlash after he talked about that March 2025 dinner at the White House on his HBO show, "Real Time."

MAHER: So meet up in person, maybe it'll be different. Spoiler alert, it was.

I reported honestly that, no, it wasn't a terrible experience at all from a guy who has done some terrible things.

KARL: And he -- and then you kept on doing what you do on your show. You didn't change, you didn't become -- you didn't become MAGA.

MAHER: Thank you for noticing, Jon, because that's what the haters pretend didn't happen.

KARL: I mean, it did, and then he starts -- I think that some of his attacks on you after the dinner are harsher than the ones that were before the dinner.

MAHER: Yes, because now he feels betrayed, which is silly because there was never a deal. It was only set up as, instead of shouting at each other, talk to each other.

KARL (voice-over): In Maher's "Club Random" podcast studio, he has a framed list of all of the ways Trump has insulted him, a list that he had the president signed.

MAHER: Just the idea, these many different ways, off the top of his head, over years.

KARL: And that list of 56 or whatever insults would have to be longer now.

MAHER: Exactly. There's an addendum. And it's available for $9.99 at BillMaher.com. It is on my Web site.

KARL: Yes.

KARL: (voice-over): Maher recently had Vice President J.D. Vance as a guest on "Real Time."

MAHER: Here's my deal breaker for your side. Okay?

J.D. VANCE, VICE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES: Okay.

MAHER: Under Trump, you guys have two outcomes in an election can be. Either we win or they cheated.

This stuff that's going on now, as I said to the vice president, this (EXPLETIVE DELETED) has to stop.

KARL: Yes. Yes, you were specifically talking about this, like the sore loser syndrome. It's -- the election is only I won, or you cheated, which is -- perfectly summarizes the way Trump has done this.

MAHER: Thank you. Yes. Exactly, there's only two outcomes. I won, you cheated.

KARL: And you pushed J.D. Vance on this, he did not --

MAHER: No, that's what I love about those Republicans. The first thing I said to him is, it's so odd, isn't it, that I didn't vote for you, and yet you guys come to the show and take your beating like a man. The Democrats don't come, and yet they got my vote. It's just odd, isn't it?

KARL: Yes, why is that? So what is that all about? I mean, and by the way, you get some Democrats, but --

MAHER: Democrats are cowardly.

KARL: Yes.

MAHER: They're cowardly. Their party is being taken over now by, you know, every day I hear about a new very radical. I feel very good about, like, 10 whenever years ago, like, I did lose fans because, you know, I wasn't going to go along with some of this crazy stuff on the left, too. I didn't change really on what I thought about the right, but just, I can't sit and just not notice stuff, which people seem to want to do because it's all about my team or your team. But yes, there's some crazy stuff, you know, when we're cheering for the Intifada, God, I'm out.

KARL: Well, I don't know if you saw it, Jay Clayton is nominated to be the head director of National Intelligence, had a hearing, just had a hearing.

MAHER: No. I'm on vacation.

KARL: And he was asked, who won the 2020 election? Did Joe Biden win the 2020 election? And he cannot answer. Now, Jay Clayton is a very serious guy with serious credentials, serious lawyer, former prosecutor, and he can't say who won the 2020 election.

MAHER: Neither could Vice President Vance on my show.

KARL: On your show.

MAHER: Yes. They can't because they know he's watching. They know where their bread is buttered. What's important to JD Vance who, by the way, we had a good time. I had a good time with him, too. You know? These are people. I always say it. You know, everybody is a monster until you talk to them. You can disagree with them a lot. But, you know, he has to do that. Trump is watching.

And there's a kind of a winking thing with those kind of guys. You know, it's like, you know he's crazy. I know he is crazy. I know you're saying this because you have to because he's watching. You know I know.

KARL: Yes, yes.

MAHER: And let's just not, like, pretend this is the end of the world because this is just what the world is. Now let's move on to something substantive.

KARL: But it is a problem if you have an entire political party, an entire movement that doesn't recognize the legitimacy of elections.

MAHER: Of course. It's been my big issue from the beginning before he was elected even the first time.

KARL: You told J.D. Vance you're open, your vote is up for grabs.

MAHER: Yes, my vote is in play because it can't be Trump running, so I'm not living in communist America. I mean, I know that the talking point is, it's not communism, it's socialism. OK. I've read the quotes from the DSA --

KARL: Oh, yeah.

MAHER: -- platform, from their own mouths. Don't tell me I'm now seeing what I am seeing. And DSA, again, they say things like, you know, takeover of key industries, government -- that's communism. You know, there is a definition.

KARL: By the way, Trump's doing that too.

MAHER: Of course. Yes.

KARL: And -- and -- and to a degree that we haven't seen any other president, Democrat or Republican, do.

MAHER: No -- that's crazy, too.

KARL: He's got a piece of Intel.

MAHER: Right.

(CROSSTALK)

KARL: He's got (ph) a piece of the A.I. companies.

MAHER: He treats everything like it's a real estate deal, or I don't know, if he's an agent or something.

(LAUGH)

MAHER: He always wants 10 or 15 percent.

KARL: So you want to see Democrats win in the midterms?

MAHER: Absolutely, and they will, because it will still be a referendum on Trump. So I think the Democrats will do very well in the midterms. 2028 is a different story because by then, this wing of the party, this new wing with all the energy, and it's not just a few people anymore. I read, every day I read about a new person in some Colorado and Wisconsin, somebody who is saying some variation of not defund the police, abolish the police. No prisons, no police, like what world do they think we could possibly live in under these conditions? It's just a level of nutty that I'm so glad that whenever it was, I was like no, I'm not going along because this is where it ends.

KARL: Could you see yourself voting for J.D. Vance?

MAHER: Yes. If this is the -- the Democratic side, yes.

KARL: Now, you have interviewed several of the possible Democratic candidates for 2028. How do you assess? Who do you like?

MAHER: Oh, I'm not going to ruin future guests by telling you that, Jon? How ridiculous.

(LAUGH)

MAHER: They're all great.

(LAUGH)

KARL: Especially the ones you haven't talked to yet. See, they got to come on the show.

MAHER: I hope we can have an eight-person presidency next time because I can't pick between this crop of geniuses.

(LAUGH)

MAHER: No, there's some very talented people. And my problem is, like I told you, the people, a lot of people on the left won't come. Everybody on the right comes.

KARL: All right. Our thanks to Bill Maher. This year's Mark Twain Prize ceremony starts streaming on Netflix on Tuesday. We'll be right back.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

KARL: That is all for today. Thanks for sharing part of your Sunday with us. Check out "World News Tonight" and have a great day.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

END

Intern FAQs

Interns must be at least 18 years of age and reside in Maine for the duration of the internship.

Internships through this program pay a minimum of $18 per hour.

Internships are 240 hours total duration. The work schedule will depend on the position and employer needs.

Internships will cover a wide range of sectors and activities. These will vary depending on what each employer has available. Examples include:

Clean energy generation: Jobs related to the production of energy from renewable sources, such as solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, and biomass. Examples include solar panel installers, wind turbine technicians, hydroelectric power plant operators, carpenters, electricians, and chemical/biological engineers.

Energy efficiency: Jobs that help to reduce energy consumption and improve energy efficiency, such as designing and implementing energy-efficient buildings, appliances, and lighting systems. Examples include weatherization technicians, HVAC technicians, energy auditors, energy managers, and building automation specialists.

Alternative transportation: Jobs related to the development and implementation of clean transportation, such as electric vehicles, public transit systems, and bike-sharing programs. Examples include electric vehicle mechanics and engineers as well as transportation planners.

Clean grid and storage: Jobs related to the development and maintenance of energy storage systems and smart grid technologies. Examples include grid operators, energy storage system technicians, and smart grid analysts.

Services: Clean energy service-related positions support the development, implementation, and regulation of clean energy technologies and policies. Examples include consultants, regulatory affairs specialists, and energy policy analysts.

text:
This article was produced in collaboration with the Food & Environment Reporting Network, an independent, nonprofit news organization.

MT. VERNON, Iowa — Chris Jones, the 65-year-old Democratic nominee for Iowa secretary of agriculture, stands at the edge of a pond on a 72-acre farm in eastern Iowa. “What you see here is how fertile Iowa is,” he says, looking intently into the water. Massive bluegills dart about in the clear depths. “When we go up to a corn or soy field, we don’t see this anymore.”

Jones isn’t just talking about the fish. He means the water’s clarity. Iowa’s lakes and ponds are often murky and fetid from algae blooms fed by fertilizer runoff, a byproduct of the state’s vast agricultural industry’s reliance on farming chemicals. Jones spent about a decade as a research engineer, monitoring the state’s rivers and streams. What he learned in that role about Iowa’s water is what spurred his run for office.

In recent years, Iowa’s cancer rate has climbed significantly above the U.S. average. It now stands as the nation’s second highest, and Iowa is one of only three states where the rate is rising. The situation has put a spotlight on nitrates, which are linked to a growing body of science to kidney, brain and ovarian cancer. Nitrates are a key component in the deluge of chemical pesticides and fertilizers used by the state’s farmers, some of which washes off farm fields and into waterways. A second culprit is glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, the world’s most common weedkiller, which the International Agency for Research on Cancer declared “probably carcinogenic” in 2015, an assessment rejected by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Historically, candidates for state-wide office in Iowa, from governor to agriculture secretary, Republican or Democrat, have avoided criticizing the agriculture industry, opting instead for platitudes about how Iowa’s farms “feed the world.” This year is different. Voters are steaming mad, and candidates on both sides of the political aisle are pointing fingers at Big Ag — and winning.

And in a change that has drawn national attention, some of those winning candidates are Democrats. The water crisis and the shifting views of agriculture are scrambling Iowa’s politics, including its traditional partisan divides. In last month’s primary, voters delivered surprises to candidates on both the Republican and Democratic sides of the ballot.

In the Republican primary for governor, a businessman, farmer and political operative named Zach Lahn shocked the political establishment by edging out Trump-endorsed Rep. Randy Feenstra for the nomination. Lahn won, in part, by openly acknowledging the state’s water crisis and connecting the dots between agriculture and cancer. Lahn was also the first candidate for statewide office endorsed by MAHA Action, the main PAC supporting Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement. MAHA voters supported Kennedy and President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential elections, but have since rebelled against some of their moves, especially the Trump administration’s open support for glyphosate. (Trump has since endorsed Lahn, declaring him an “America First Patriot” and an “effective Voice for Iowa Agriculture.”)

“I could get into tears thinking about the people that I know that have gotten cancer,” Lahn told Tucker Carlson in a February interview.

As for the Democrats, they have their best shot in a decade or more of winning statewide offices in November’s election. Democrat Josh Turek is neck-and-neck in recent polling with Republican Ashley Hinson in the open race for U.S. Senate. And Lahn’s Democratic opponent, Rob Sand, bested him by one percentage point, within the margin of error, in recent polling in the governor’s race.

And then there’s Chris Jones. His bid to become secretary of agriculture — as a Democrat —may be the most unexpected development so far. He’s running an insurgent campaign in a deep red state to reduce the agriculture industry’s dependence on toxic chemicals, crack down on large livestock confinements, and most important: to clean up the water.

The farm he is visiting raises a variety of vegetables in unruly, green gardens: peppers, sweet corn, green beans, potatoes and collards. Though the farmer grows soybeans on some of the property to make ends meet, other fields have been allowed to return to marshy wetland. It’s a sharp contrast to the corn and soybean fields that carpet most of Iowa’s farmland, geometrically arrayed and stretching from fence row to fence row.

Jones admits this farm looks a bit “chaotic,” especially when compared to one of its huge, conventional counterparts. Those farms, Jones says, are an attempt to control nature, and “what has controlling nature here done for us?” He turns back to the pond. “It’s polluted all our water. It’s really destroyed a lot of Iowa.”

His Republican opponent is the incumbent secretary of agriculture, Mike Naig, who can’t really run on water. That’s because, of all things, he actually worked as the manager of state and local government affairs in Iowa for Monsanto, the maker of the widely used herbicide Roundup, which is now owned by Bayer. Naig puts a sunny spin on the water problem, doubling down on the state’s voluntary approach to cajoling farmers to pollute less while insisting that things are getting better — a claim that isn’t backed by data collected from waterways. “We have made tremendous progress working with farmers and landowners and hundreds of public and private partners to incorporate responsible farming practices, but there’s no finish line when it comes to conservation,” he said, in a June press release. (Naig did not respond to a request for comment sent to his campaign.)

Jones is at the vanguard of a crop of Democrats who see a new political opening in rural and red states, trying to make a case that Republican policies have not well served the voters of states like Iowa who are living with the consequences — from tariffs on agriculture to the shuttering of rural hospitals to stagnant wages and rising prices. But none of those issues seem to have galvanized Iowa’s electorate like the state’s polluted water and rising cancer rates.

The possibility that Jones and other Democrats have a chance to win, in a state so dominated by Republicans for two decades, is due in no small part to the motivating power of the water crisis.

“Cancer doesn’t care what party you belong to,” Jones said. “Republicans don’t like drinking poisonous water any more than Democrats do.”

Iowa’s water problem — and the political reckoning it’s triggering — has been building for years.

In 2015, the Des Moines Water Works, which was spending well over $1 million a year to filter pollutants from the city’s water, filed a federal lawsuit accusing the governing boards of three upstream rural counties of allowing high levels of nitrate runoff into the Raccoon River, which, along with the Des Moines River, provides drinking water to the city of Des Moines. Two years later, the case was dismissed, with the judge ruling that the entities named in the suit lacked the authority to control farm pollution.

At the time, Jones had just started managing a state-funded network of more than 70 sensors on rivers and streams across Iowa. The data he collected found Iowa’s water routinely contained heightened levels of two chemicals prevalent in the fertilizer and manure farmers apply to their fields every year: phosphorus, known to trigger toxic algae blooms in freshwater lakes and ponds; and nitrate, suspected of being carcinogenic at low levels in drinking water. Many academics might have been satisfied to quietly publish the findings on a little-viewed website, but Jones spoke up. In academic papers, at community meetings, a hard-hitting blog, a podcast, and in a 2023 book, he methodically tied the state’s water-quality crisis directly to agriculture.

The EPA requires municipal water systems to cap nitrate at 10 parts per million — a level that Iowa water agencies often barely manage to meet. (Importantly for rural areas, the EPA offers no standards to protect people who rely on private wells, which nearly 10 percent of Iowans do.) But a body of evidence from National Cancer Institute researchers suggests regular consumption of water with nitrate levels even significantly lower than 10 parts per million still boosts cancer risk.

A March 2026 Iowa Environment Council report, co-authored by some of the state’s leading oncologists and environmental-health experts, illustrates how Iowa’s “toxic mix” of environmental risk factors contribute to the increased cancer rate, which federal data show started rising beyond the national average in 2008. That mix includes nitrate, which can leech into groundwater from fertilizer and manure; pesticides and herbicides, used to protect crops; and PFAS, the so-called forever chemicals that were often found in sewage sludge spread on farm fields as fertilizer. Iowa farmers spray up to 32 million pounds of glyphosate each year, not to mention heavy doses of other herbicides including atrazine, acetochlor and 2, 4-D. There are also elevated levels of the radioactive gas radon, which is naturally occurring in Iowa soil and the second leading cause of lung cancer in the U.S. But exposure to radon can’t explain the rise in cancer cases, because its levels are constant. Iowa’s agriculture output, however, has intensified in recent decades along with its cancer rates.

“This shows us that there’s many aspects of the way in which we are using our land that are known or suspected risk factors for cancer,” says David Cwiertny, who directs the Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination at the University of Iowa.

Iowans have taken note. In a February 2026 poll Iowa voters named cancer their top concern —ahead of cost of living, and then, clean water. “People are finally beginning to understand that there’s implications for folks here in Iowa,” Cwiertny says, adding that Jones, his former colleague, deserves at least some of the credit for that.

In 2015, Jones started writing a blog where he documented his research on water quality. It slowly gained a statewide readership in progressive circles, and as it did, Jones began making each post “a little more provocative,” as he puts it — inserting commentary about what agriculture might have to do with it. Over time, the blog developed a sharp critique of the state’s voluntary water-quality rules and a haves-vs.-have-nots narrative of wealthy farmers and their agribusiness allies reaping profits while fouling the environment for everyone else.

It emerged as a genuine embarrassment for the agricultural powers that be. In 2022, Jones published a piece titled, “Mamas Don’t Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Farmers,” which countered the agriculture industry’s mythology of the Iowa farmer as a heroic, go-it-alone feeder-of-the-world. That myth, he argued, was a self-serving way to uphold the status quo and frame anyone who points to the state’s environmental woes as anti-farmer.

Eventually, he recalls, two state senators began to pressure the university to rein him in. When his bosses told him to stop writing “this stuff,” Jones said he’d rather retire, which is what he did. It was an example of the political power of the state’s agricultural interests.

That power is the reason that the state’s political leaders, Republican and Democratic alike, have treated Iowa’s water woes gingerly, avoiding naming Big Ag as a culprit and promoting only voluntary measures to curb pollution, which have proven to be ineffective. It’s not hard to understand the light touch. Iowa’s farmers earn more than $40 billion from selling their crops and animal products each year, second only to California. And every year, they devote more than 70 percent of the landscape to just two crops: corn and soybeans, which require a massive volume of pesticides and fertilizers. A lot of that corn and soybeans isn’t eaten by people. Instead it is either transformed into biofuels or used as feed for the state’s teeming livestock populations, which are often held in concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, housing nearly 24 million hogs, 44 million egg-laying hens, and 3.5 million cattle — more than any other state, and dwarfing Iowa’s human population of just over 3 million.

All told, Iowa farmers spend around $8.7 billion each year on pesticides, fertilizers, seeds and machinery such as combines, making them a crucial market for global agribusiness firms Bayer and Syngenta, the fertilizer firm CF Industries and farm-equipment maker John Deere. These enormous, powerful firms have a stake in maintaining the current regulation-light status quo.

But, as Jones noted at a recent fundraiser, despite the state’s status as an agricultural powerhouse, its farmers aren’t actually a potent voting force. The state is home to only about 160,000 full-time farmers, according to the 2022 Agricultural Census. And a far smaller fraction run operations large enough to have a stake in the status quo Jones wants to shake up. The census also found that only 11 percent of Iowa’s 87,000 farms had annual sales of at least $1 million — and that top 11 percent accounts for nearly three-quarters of the state’s total sales of agriculture products. By contrast, nearly half of the state’s farms had sales of less than $50,000, accounting for less than 1 percent of sales. In short, the big farms are doing the most business and the most damage — and at least in theory, there aren’t enough of them to truly swing the vote in a state with 1.8 million active registered voters.

The other knock against Jones, in addition to being a Democrat, is his lack of family ties to farming — a rarity among ag-secretary candidates. Naig’s bio on the Iowa Department of Agriculture website notes that he grew up on a farm and is still involved in its operation today. The implication is that, unlike Jones, Naig has deep ties to Iowa’s heroic farmers. However, Jones doesn’t come off as an out-of-touch professorial type. He’s an Iowa native who speaks bluntly and who grew up fishing, and who to this day spends his spare time in and around Iowa’s waterways, pole in hand. So he may cut a more appealing figure in rural Iowa than Republicans bargain for.

And Jones has a handy prop for turning Naig’s own backstory into a liability. At campaign events, he likes to show off a memento he picked up years before: Naig’s business card from his days as a Monsanto lobbyist, which he gave Jones when Jones was working for the Iowa Soybean Association. In April, Jones posted a meme on his social media accounts that depicted the race as a battle between “Monsanto Mike” and “Clean Water Chris.”

It’s a strong frame that seems like it should appeal to voters across the state. But the real vulnerability for Jones is not that he doesn’t farm — it’s that he’s associated with cities. And the big divide in Iowa, as in lots of places around the country, is between urban and rural.

Still, this disadvantage has an upside. Iowa is heavily rural, but maybe not as rural as the perception: 63 percent of its population lives in urban areas. Jones’ path to victory involves rallying urbanites without a direct interest in agriculture to vote for clean water. But he also needs to peel off some of the rural vote, which Trump won overwhelmingly in 2024, to push him over the top.

Jones understands this, and he thinks the water issue allows him to do that. “Only 14 percent of rural Iowa is comprised of farmers and their wives,” he says. “Most of rural Iowa is nurses and truck drivers and teachers and hairdressers and people who work at convenience stores.”

All Iowans feel the burden of toxic water, he argues, even as only a select few reap benefits from the operations that cause the pollution. “These environmental issues are common-good issues that affect everyone in rural Iowa, and especially those that are not farming,” Jones says. “Avoidance of water quality, avoidance of the environmental consequences of agriculture has been a real tragic mistake here for the Democratic Party.”

Lahn, the MAHA-backed GOP candidate for governor, talks about water, too, but he is a newcomer to the issue. Until relatively recently, Lahn was part of the libertarian wing of Republican politics, which isn’t focused on environmental issues. Jones has been at it for much longer and — unlike Lahn — he isn’t likely to fear breaking the political taboo against calling for major regulation of farming practices.

“The success of Lahn and Jones in the primary goes to the importance of the issues,” said fellow Ranger Zack Smith. Both sides of the aisle see water as key to winning, and it has scrambled traditional partisan divides. “It’s probably the No.1 or No.2 issue on the ballot this year.”

There is, of course, one big difference between the two men, the Rangers say. Lahn is a Republican in a red state, and Jones is not. (The candidates also hold diametrically opposed views on practically every political, social and economic issue that doesn’t involve water.) Because of that, the Rangers said, they are a little skeptical of Jones’ chances of winning office.

“He’s gonna get spun as that ‘liberal environmentalist wacko’ that’s trying to put farmers out of business,” Bormann says. Smith gives Jones more of a shot. He expects Naig to dominate the farmer vote, but believes that Jones may have enough support in populous urban counties to make things interesting. “I think it’s going to be a closer race than a lot of people think.”

Art Cullen, who has edited the Storm Lake Times Pilot in south-central Iowa since 1990, won the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for a series of scathing editorials on agriculture’s role in the water crisis. He says Jones’ clean-water message is genuinely popular among Iowans. “But for whatever reason, whether it’s abortion or whatever the case, they vote for Republican majorities that refuse to give them clean water,” Cullen says. And he doesn’t see Jones changing that: “It’s going to be very difficult for Chris to beat Mike Naig. He’s running against an amicable, or amiable, Republican Farm Bureau guy, and Iowa loves incumbents.”

But at a moment that voters across the country are in an anti-incumbent mood, the question is whether Iowans’ anger over water and cancer, combined with a more general national predisposition to overthrow status quo candidates, will change the equation for long-time Republican voters.

Bill Billings, 62, a healthcare administrator and the former mayor of Red Oak, a town of about 5,600 in western Iowa, may be an example of that voter. He was diagnosed in 2024 with a rare cancer called high-grade B-cell lymphoma. “I was the healthiest cancer patient that my cancer team says they’ve ever had,” he says. He only occasionally drinks alcohol, “eats clean,” exercises daily, and in a previous career worked as a conditioning coach for college athletes.

Today, he carefully filters his water to remove nitrates, but his lifestyle still includes one risk factor that he ties to his cancer: Red Oak is surrounded on all sides by large corn and soybean operations, the closest less than a mile away. He says his proximity subjects him to pesticide vapor from the crop-dusting aircraft that often traverse the sky nearby, as well as “any herbicides or pesticides that I used around my home” in landscaping. (His cancer is in remission after chemotherapy.)

Glyphosate stands out for him in particular. It’s suspected of boosting risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a category that includes B-cell lymphoma. And Billings says he sees the malady all around him. When he was first diagnosed, “My oncology team said that they were treating upwards of 20 patients for basically the same form of cancer that I have.” These days, he knows two people who live nearby with the same cancer type. “I would say you can’t find anybody in the state of Iowa who doesn’t have a family member or a close acquaintance” with a cancer story.

text:
by Willy Blackmore

For decades, highways and industrial corridors have exposed Black communities to disproportionate levels of diesel pollution. As the Trump administration eases clean truck standards, environmental advocates warn those neighborhoods could once again pay the highest price.

The research is conclusive: Black communities are disproportionately exposed to diesel exhaust and other traffic-related pollution. So when Biden-era crackdowns on diesel emissions were scheduled to take effect, Black neighborhoods near freeways or industrial corridors anticipated breathing easier.

But a new move by the Environmental Protection Agency could mean the air in those communities could get worse, and soon.

LEARN MORE: Texas Keeps Greenlighting Pollution. Guess Who Lives Nearby

The Trump administration has announced it is pushing back or adjusting diesel emission restrictions that had been tightened under President Joe Biden, calling the regulations “unnecessary and unworkable.” Originally announced in 2023 and set to take effect this year, the regulations would have required trucks and other diesel engines to use more advanced, emissions-reducing technology.

No Data on Health

In a statement earlier this month, the EPA said the change will save truckers some $12 billion, including up to $6,152 per diesel engine subject to the regulations. American consumers and households would reap the benefits, according to the statement.

“Collectively, these savings will be passed on to American families through lower costs for food, household goods, and other products trucks deliver, while still maintaining strong environmental protections and ensuring clean air,” according to the statement.

The agency did not calculate how the changes would affect human health.

Under Biden, the E.P.A. estimated that 72 million people lived within a mile of a truck freight route, increasing their exposure to unhealthy air. The study found that Black people and those with lower incomes were more likely to live in these areas.

Semi-trucks, buses, and other heavy-duty vehicles only make up a small portion of the vehicles on American roads and highways. They are more likely to pollute the air in neighboring communities, which are often home to Black and brown people.

Semi-trucks, buses, and other heavy-duty vehicles only make up a small portion of the vehicles on American roads and highways. They are more likely to pollute the air in neighboring communities, which are often home to Black and brown people.

But because of their larger, often diesel-powered engines, heavy-duty vehicles account for a disproportionate amount of the pollution emitted by the transportation sector.

The heavy-duty fleet accounts for 45% of smog-forming nitrogen oxide emissions – pollution that the Biden Administration made efforts to curtail with so-called clean truck standards.

Environmental groups were quick to point out that the rollback would harm public health.

“Clean truck standards save lives,” Katherine García, director of the Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All campaign, said in a statement. “Weakening them would mean more toxic pollution in the air and more families paying the price with their health.”

Black Communities Hurt Most

There’s a substantial amount of research that shows how emissions from trucking and other heavy-duty vehicles are particularly harmful to Black families.

A Union of Concerned Scientists report from 2019 found that people of color living in the Northeast were exposed to 66% more pollution from vehicles — including a disproportionate amount emitted by a small number of heavy-duty vehicles — than white residents.

The higher levels of exposure are part of the legacy of redlining, which clustered Black households in less desirable parts of cities. That included neighborhoods developed near factories, freeways, and industrial corridors.

Environmental groups objecting to the change also noted that technological developments are making it substantially easier to cut emissions from heavy-duty fleets.

RELATED: Formaldehyde Is Everywhere. Get Ready to Breathe More of It

Peter Zalzal, associate vice president for the Environmental Defense Fund, said in a statement that diesel engines “emit huge amounts of smog- and soot-forming pollution into the air we breathe.” But vehicle manufacturers, he said, “are already introducing new engines that can substantially cut this pollution and meet protective standards.”

The EPA “should abandon this proposal and instead maintain strong pollution safeguards for new heavy-duty vehicles,” Zalzal said.
