text:
Indiana Department of Environmental Management officials are excited to advance a new state-led coal ash program to strengthen regulations.

However, some cleanup advocates still worry that potential federal changes might hinder the state’s ability to do much.

“The federal coal ash rule is basically a carbon copy of what the Indiana state program will be,” said Ashley Williams, executive director for Just Transition Northwest Indiana. “With the Indiana program, its hands are really tied because the state coal ash rule must be identical to the federal rule.”

On June 30, IDEM announced that its submitted a state coal combustion residuals permit to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for approval. The department has worked on the program’s plan for about a year to year-and-a-half, and the process included public feedback and multiple iterations of the final proposal.

The plan, if approved by the EPA, would direct IDEM to create a permitting section with about nine to 13 staff members to address coal ash impoundment closure permit applications. It would also require any facility with coal ash units as defined by a federal rule to obtain a state permit.

Coal ash is a byproduct that is primarily created from burning coal in power plants, according to the EPA. It contains toxic heavy metals, including arsenic, boron, lithium, molybdenum and radium, which can interfere with child development and cause cancer.

According to IDEM, the agency estimates that more than 100 coal ash units statewide would require permitting under the EPA’s current rule, which would make Indiana the largest permitting program nationwide.

“We’ve put a ton of work and effort into this,” said Brian Wolff, IDEM’s assistant commissioner. “We think that there’s a lot of benefits for both environmentally and to the public and regulatory community as well.”

Wolff said it requires operators to close coal ash sites properly to protect both human health and the environment. He also thinks it will provide a lot of predictability and flexibility for specific site conditions.

“Geologically speaking, certain areas of the state of Indiana can be very, very different,” Wolff said. “A part up in the Lake Michigan basin could be very different from something down along the Ohio River. This gives us the ability to create conditions for closure that are site-specific and not just have to do a ‘one size fits all’ approach.”

IDEM’s program announcement comes at a time when the EPA is likely to make amendments to its coal ash cleanup requirements, which cleanup advocates have said is a betrayal to vulnerable communities nationwide.

On April 9, the EPA announced proposals to amend federal regulations focused on the disposal of coal ash in landfills and surface impoundments, according to the agency. Proposed rule changes would dismantle coal ash protections for operating and former coal power plants, exempt hundreds of coal ash dumps from regulation and permit owners of coal plants to minimize, delay or avoid contamination cleanup, according to Earthjustice.

The EPA accepted public comments on its new rule through June 29. The federal agency has not indicated when a decision will be made.

Seeing changes that the EPA wants to make to its coal ash rule makes Williams nervous for Indiana’s future cleanup, she said. She feels vulnerable areas have faced continual environmental justice blows.

“It’s a tough pill for me to swallow,” Williams said, “as both a Michigan City resident and as executive director of an environmental nonprofit whose very inception was to see that there would be a complete cleanup and closure of the Michigan City Generating station and coal ash sites across the state.”

On Wednesday, Earthjustice announced that President Donald Trump’s administration published an advance notice of proposed rulemaking that would result in more coal ash pollution. The EPA, according to Earthjustice, is “floating the idea” of letting coal plants “essentially permit themselves and take advantage of the grossly weakened provisions of its proposed coal ash rule.”

A comment period is running through the end of the month for the proposed rulemaking.

“The EPA appears to be motivated to get this finalized in a short time,” said Lisa Evans, senior counsel for Earthjustice. “They’re moving forward quickly on all cylinders.”

Although Evans thinks Indiana’s proposed coal ash plan is positive, she also has concerns for what the future holds, especially since the state’s plan cannot be more stringent than the federal rule.

Wolff said IDEM might change its rule to follow what the EPA chooses to do. However, there’s some scenarios where IDEM won’t have to follow suit.

“If (the EPA wants) a general permit, but they’ve already delegated it to us or we’re in the process of delegation, we wouldn’t necessarily have to follow the general permit program,” Wolff said. “It also depends on when things are finalized federally. If we have delegation, and we’re issuing permits, once we’ve issued a permit, they’re kind of locked into the permit conditions.”

Environmental groups statewide have been supportive of IDEM’s coal ash program goals, Wolff said.

Indra Frank, coal ash advisor for the Hoosier Environmental Council, said the current rule sent to the EPA is in good shape and will protect both human health and the environment well.

But, Frank is still concerned that IDEM’s coal ash rule have to be basically identical to federal rules.

“The EPA has proposed some really awful changes to the federal rule,” Frank said. “If the federal rule changes, then Indiana law will force Indiana to have those same changes. … The changes they made will increase coal ash pollution.”

Frank has three main concerns with EPA’s proposals, including that it would leave about half of Indiana’s coal ash with no requirements, reduce requirements for those being cleaned, and allow coal ash to be stored in dangerous ways.

“For example, they were proposing to allow coal ash piles for an indeterminate period of time,” Frank said. “Well, a pile of coal ash could be open to the wind, and then you’ve got coal ash blowing in the wind, and that’s a significant inhalation hazard.”

The EPA’s proposal would also allow coal ash to be disposed of in contact with groundwater, which Frank said can contaminate other water. In an ideal world, Frank said she’d keep Indiana’s coal ash practices as is.

Williams worries that once a federal rule is finalized, Indiana’s coal ash program will be a false promise to communities like Michigan City who need cleanup.

“It’s absolutely not going to be strengthening protections for communities across the country, especially with Hoosiers,” Williams said. “I just don’t see how Indiana is going to see any expansion of extra protections or seeing due diligence and cleanup of these sites under the new coal ash rule.”

text:
ODESSA, Texas — A vital energy relationship binding the United States and Mexico is facing unprecedented uncertainty. For decades, a vast network of cross-border pipelines has quietly driven Mexico’s industrial sector and power grid, delivering the lion’s share of its natural gas. Today, that interdependence is under threat as the Trump administration shifts its stance on the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Instead of a traditional renewal of the free-trade pact, Trump administration officials announced they intend to negotiate trade amendments on an annual basis for the next decade until the USMCA officially expires in 2036. This policy pivot, coupled with escalating global market volatility from ongoing conflicts like the U.S.–Iran war, has energy experts warning of serious disruptions to North American energy security.

Mexico’s reliance on American energy has grown exponentially over the last twenty years. In 2005, Mexico imported 750 million cubic feet of natural gas per day from the U.S. By last year, that figure skyrocketed to 7.5 billion cubic feet daily, with at least 90% of the supply originating from Texas, primarily extracted from the oil-rich Permian Basin. According to Mexico’s Energy Secretary, Luz Elena González Escobar, the country currently imports roughly 75% of all the natural gas it consumes.

In response to this vulnerability, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo’s administration announced plans to ramp up domestic fracking to foster energy independence. However, energy analysts remain highly skeptical. Experts argue that reversing decades of underinvestment in state-run Pemex, which historically prioritized lucrative crude oil over natural gas infrastructure, will take years.

The immediate fallout of an unraveling USMCA could severely damage both economies. For Texas producers, Mexico offers a crucial outlet for disposing of excess natural gas reserves.

For Mexico, cheap pipeline gas is fundamental to economic survival. While Texas maintains storage facilities capable of holding excess reserves for up to 100 days, Mexico holds a mere three-day emergency buffer. If trade protections erode, Mexico faces soaring electricity costs, leaving its manufacturing competitiveness exposed to geopolitical crossfire.

Kirk Lippold, a national security expert and former commander of the USS Cole, said radar operators are trained to differentiate a live track — anything from a boat or a submarine periscope to an inbound drone or missile — from clutter. If drones aren't detected before they reach a wind farm, "we have bigger national security issues," he said.

Trump administration says there are new risks

According to the Department of Justice, defense officials gave the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management classified information in November 2025 detailing new national security risks from offshore wind projects.

BOEM halted construction on five big East Coast projects days before Christmas. Burgum said they had to address the rapid evolution of relevant adversary technologies and vulnerabilities created by these projects near East Coast cities. This came after courts blocked Trump's efforts to halt development through executive action.

READ MORE: Construction finishes on a major Massachusetts offshore wind farm, the first during Trump's time in office

Like the United States, Sweden is raising security concerns with offshore wind energy. Officials said Thursday they're approving two offshore wind farms while rejecting 11 others.

Green Power Sweden CEO Nils Grunditz said he questions why Sweden is scaling back its offshore wind plans when technological solutions for radar interference are used elsewhere in the region. Denmark has been a pioneer in wind energy since building the first offshore wind farm in 1991.

The UK government said in March it bought new air defense radars to mitigate against anomalies created by offshore wind farms, touting it as new technology that secures coexistence of air defense and offshore wind. The independent climate change think tank E3G said North Sea turbines can be a defense asset, for example by including surveillance and monitoring equipment.

Judges were not convinced by the Trump administration

Developers impacted by the construction freeze and states sued. The DOJ argued national security concerns are paramount and federal courts do not second-guess military officials' assessment of these risks.

Federal judges reviewed the classified information and allowed all five wind farms to resume construction.

READ MORE: Judge clears way for New York offshore wind project, handing industry another victory against Trump

At the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, Senior Judge Royce Lamberth expressed concern that the stated national security reasoning may have been "pretextual," to mask the true motives for stopping offshore wind.

In putting a major wind farm for Rhode Island and Connecticut back on track in January, Lamberth said the government did not apply the newly discovered concerns specifically to that project, Revolution Wind, Burgum publicly criticized offshore wind around the time of the stop work order for reasons unrelated to national security, and BOEM waited to act until December on information it received in November.

READ MORE: Trump's offshore wind project freeze hit with lawsuits from states and developers

The Pentagon is also holding up the development of onshore wind farms, and the administration has used emergency orders to keep fossil fuel plants online. On Thursday, attorneys general from 18 states and Washington moved to intervene in a lawsuit to try to advance the onshore wind farms.

Meghan Greenfield, a partner at Jenner & Block LLP in Washington, said the administration is making a national security argument in so many different contexts, "it has caused increased skepticism by the courts."

A retired Navy officer is suspicious of the administration's motives

In buying back offshore wind leases, the Interior Department cited national security concerns with the projects, including those off California. The Interior Department said Thursday there were serious national security risks that demanded immediate attention, and it won't let "reckless projects create higher utility costs, a weakened energy system and unnecessary harm to the environment." Several states are suing.

Retired U.S. Navy Vice Adm. Dennis McGinn knows the waters off California's shore well. He commanded the fleet responsible for naval operations across the eastern and northern Pacific Ocean. He said there's no "showstopping national security issue" that would invalidate years of analysis of the lease areas.

McGinn said he thinks the administration is maximizing the risks and costs of offshore wind while minimizing the benefits to justify pursuing more fossil fuels and "it doesn't pass commonsense tests." Offshore wind produces electricity cleanly. Oil, coal and natural gas emit carbon pollution when burned.

McGinn, who served as an assistant secretary of the Navy, said that radar interference is a problem recognized early on and adequately addressed and that thousands of turbines are operating across Europe and Asia.

"National security and offshore wind are compatible, if it is done right, in the right locations," he said.

Economist Diana Furchtgott-Roth disagrees. A distinguished fellow at the Energy Policy Research Foundation, Furchtgott-Roth said the defense issues have been known for decades, the military's views should be taken very seriously, the nation shouldn't be dependent on Chinese-made turbines, and gas, coal and nuclear provide affordable, reliable power. The administration is acting prudently, she said.

Members of Congress were briefed

Democratic U.S. Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island said he participated in a classified briefing months ago and didn't find the reasoning compelling. Reed, the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, is trying to include a measure in the defense bill that sets military policy to force a 180-day deadline for a military office known as the siting clearinghouse to evaluate wind projects and explain its conclusion.

"They have to be able to produce a thoughtful and thorough analysis which justifies their decision," Reed said Wednesday. "That's the way to go."

Even with that step, Reed said, this administration finds many ways to stop things it doesn't like and he expects the campaign against wind energy to continue.

WASHINGTON — More than a dozen Senate Democrats are launching an investigation into the Trump administration’s efforts to kill offshore wind energy projects, specifically targeting a series of lease buyout agreements signed by project developers.

The investigation is being led by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Angus King, I-Maine, an independent who caucuses with the democrats.

In a letter to the heads of wind farm developers TotalEnergies, Ocean Winds, Duke Energy and Invenergy, the senators express “deep concern” over the companies’ voluntary termination of nine leases to develop offshore wind farms in the United States.

According to the senators, the Trump administration has paid out more than $2.7 billion in taxpayer dollars to entice the companies to abandon their projects.

They also expressed concern that these decisions “will harm grid reliability, job opportunities, and economic development in states across the country.”

“These buyouts have been announced amid a larger effort by the Trump Administration to stall wind and solar projects — the energy sources that are cheap, clean, and fastest to bring online — across the country,” the senators wrote.

“At a time when gas prices have spiked by an average of more than $1 dollar per gallon due to the President’s war in Iran and electricity prices are rising nearly twice as fast as inflation, clean energy offers a critical opportunity to reduce our dependence on fossil fuels and relieve costs for people across the country,” they continued.

“Dismantling the burgeoning offshore wind industry now and creating broader uncertainty for investment in cheap, clean energy will have consequences for decades to come,” they said.

Interior Department officials insist none of this is true, and that the money provided to the companies was merely a refund of what they paid for the leases.

In return, most if not all of the companies have vowed to reinvest the funds in other, nonrenewable energy projects.

The senators called on the companies to turn over internal communications and posed a series of questions: whether the administration had raised legitimate national security concerns; whether the companies had struck a deal with the Department of the Interior involving a pledge to invest in fossil fuel projects; and whether any conditions were attached to the payouts.

The letters were also signed by Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Chris Coons, D-Del., John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., Ed Markey, D-Mass., Adam Schiff, D-Calif., Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., Peter Welch, D-Vt., Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.

description:

The federal government is expected to establish new rules that will take effect in 2027 regarding river water allocations.
The red dashed line shows that under “Probable Minimum” projections, Lake Mead would drop below 1,000 feet by June 2028.
If the federal government continues to prioritize Lake Powell, that’s water that won’t be sent downstream to Lake Mead, possibly amplifying the effects on Lake Mead.

text:
LAS VEGAS (KLAS) – A critical year is ahead for the nation’s two largest reservoirs, with no relief after a record-low snowpack and a continuing drought.

A comment posted on the Colorado River Basin’s Facebook page Wednesday morning might have said it best: “Not enough water in the Monsoons to help. There’s only 2 things that can save Mead and Powell right now: 150 percent Colorado Rockies snow pack for 5 consecutive years, or God himself.”

Projections released earlier this week show Lake Mead dropping to the lowest levels seen since Hoover Dam was built in the 1930s, falling to 1,035.86 feet in November. That’s about 6.5 feet lower than Lake Mead’s level Friday at noon — 1,042.52 feet. Lake Mead is the nation’s largest reservoir, but it’s currently at 27 percent capacity.

The latest projections

The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation’s 24-month study, which is updated monthly, published “most probable” lake levels through June 2028, when Lake Mead is expected to be at 1,009.69 feet. That represents a drop of nearly 33 feet over the next two years. When the lake is at “full pool,” the lake’s surface is at 1,229 feet.

Lake Powell, the second largest reservoir, is currently at 24 percent capacity. The federal government has consistently prioritized keeping Powell at levels that protect Glen Canyon Dam’s ability to produce hydroelectricity. To do so, the reservoir’s target level has been established as 3,525 feet. But Lake Powell is currently at 3,524.03 feet right now.

To keep Powell at its current level, the federal government has increased releases from Flaming Gorge Reservoir on the Utah-Wyoming border, bolstering flow in the Green River, the Colorado River’s largest tributary.

The government has also reduced releases from Lake Powell. Lower releases will have an impact on Lake Mead.

Water shortage levels that determine Colorado River allocations are based on Lake Mead’s level. And even under the most optimistic forecasts, that will mean less water for Arizona and Nevada in 2027. Those decisions are based on projections that come out in August, looking ahead at the lake’s projected level at the end of the year.

Water for the Las Vegas valley

Officials from the Southern Nevada Water Authority aren’t worried about the water supply to Las Vegas. Despite continuing growth in the valley, SNWA says Nevada is using far less than its allocation. That’s the result of water recycling and reduced use of water outdoors. SNWA receives credits for water that is recycled and returned to Lake Mead.

About 90 percent of the Las Vegas valley’s water comes from Lake Mead, with the remaining 10% from wells.

Total consumptive use of Colorado River water in Nevada is estimated to be 198,001 acre-feet in 2026 out of its 287,000-acre-foot allocation under current water shortage conditions. (An acre-foot is equal to 325,851 gallons — literally, the amount of water it takes to cover an acre in water a foot deep.)

The federal government is expected to establish new rules that will take effect in 2027 regarding river water allocations. Those rules might be released around the same time that Reclamation releases its next 24-month study in the middle of August. Current rules expire at the end of the year.

Worst-case scenario

Reclamation also released projections that show the best- and worst-case scenarios, shown in the graphic below. The red dashed line shows that under “Probable Minimum” projections, Lake Mead would drop below 1,000 feet by June 2028.

Some scientists say the “Probable Minimum” has been a more accurate reflection of actual reality during the drought that began in 2000.

Lake Powell’s place in the projections

Continued efforts to maintain Lake Powell’s elevation at 3,525 feet are not reflected in the projections released on Wednesday. Reclamation shows Lake Powell going far below that immediately in its projections with 10 consecutive months of declines that would put Powell at 3,491.75 feet.

If the federal government continues to prioritize Lake Powell, that’s water that won’t be sent downstream to Lake Mead, possibly amplifying the effects on Lake Mead.

The graphs in the slideshow below show levels at Lake Mead (the first slide) and Lake Powell compared to levels over the past five years.

The Colorado River supplies water to 40 million people, but scientists have said that climate change has reduced the amount of water in the basin by about 20%.

The result: More water is promised to users than the amount that actually exists.

The federal government — the Interior Department and the Bureau of Reclamation — are now shaping future agreements on how to manage the Colorado River after the seven states in the river basin failed to come to a consensus.

text:
To the Editor:

With the accelerating crisis of climate change on one hand, and the Trump misadventure in Iran on the other, transforming our energy economy away from fossil fuel sources is an absolute necessity. The present legal and regulatory system, however, was built around the requirements of utility companies, and presents unnecessary procedural obstacles to these essential changes.

Fossil fuel prices are going to keep rising, while the costs of renewables like solar and wind will move in the other direction. Framingham and other cities in similar situations should be able to reduce both operating costs and environmental damage without opposition from the utilities.

If Massachusetts wants to accelerate the transition to clean energy, it’s time to frame and enact new regulations focused on community benefit, not the convenience of corporate monopolies. The Distributed Energy Resource Peak Reduction Standard is an important step in lessening the bureaucratic obstacles to solar adoption, allowing affordable housing developments to live up to their description.

Warren Senders

text:
In This Issue: New Regulatory Landscapes for Battery Energy Storage Systems Emerge as the Industry, Grid Operators, and Policy Makers Explore Ways to Rapidly Deploy These Critical Assets

By Sarah Main

The U.S. energy storage market has entered a new era. In the past year, record-breaking deployment of battery energy storage systems (“BESS”), sweeping federal legislation, new state permitting regimes, and breakthrough chemistries have fundamentally reshaped the landscape for BESS developers, offtakers, and policymakers alike. In this issue of Climate Law Matters, we focus on BESS, the technology at the heart of the clean energy transition that has undergone remarkable market transformation over the last few years.

In the first quarter of 2026, the U.S. storage market installed a record 3.3 gigawatts (“GW”)/8.4 gigawatt-hours (“GWh”) of BESS. Of this, approximately 2.3 GW of capacity was attributable to utility-scale installations. The residential and commercial BESS sectors also saw record installations in Q1, largely due to pipeline projects coming online after priority projects that sought to meet tax incentive eligibility deadlines in the second half of 2025. This momentum is not likely to slow anytime soon. By 2031, installed BESS capacity in the U.S. is projected to grow by over 275%. Data centers, fleet electrification, domestic supply chain and manufacturing incentives, and the broader need to firm the grid and manage intermittent renewables are accelerating demand for BESS at a pace that was difficult to imagine just a few years ago. The current state of the market signals a bright spot for batteries in the clean energy future.

At the same time, the policy and regulatory landscape surrounding BESS has shifted in fundamental ways. BESS emerged from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (“OBBBA”) as a clear winner. The OBBBA preserved robust tax incentives for energy storage even as it pulled back support for other clean energy technologies like wind and solar. At the same time, the OBBBA introduced new challenges for BESS developers facing an already constrained supply chain for battery components. The OBBBA’s strict new Foreign Entity of Concern (“FEOC”) requirements are reshaping procurement and supply chain decisions for those seeking to qualify for tax credits.

Meanwhile, states are advancing their own regulatory and siting frameworks to support the continued deployment of BESS. For instance, Massachusetts launched an entirely new, consolidated siting and permitting regime for storage projects, effective this month, that promises to reshape how BESS facilities move from concept to construction.

These market and regulatory forces are creating new opportunities, innovations, and challenges across the BESS value chain. Developers are navigating novel permitting pathways and community engagement mandates. Data centers and hyperscalers are an expansive new market for BESS, but one that is not unaffected by a changing state and local attitudes towards these projects and their massive appetite for power. Offtakers are structuring virtual power purchase agreements to secure storage capacity. Manufacturers of other battery chemistries, like sodium-ion batteries and compressed-air storage, are coming to market as solutions to address the thermal risks and supply chain vulnerabilities of the market-dominating lithium-ion technology. And regional transmission operators are exploring use cases for BESS to alleviate transmission constraints and address reliability needs, especially amid the new compliance requirements under FERC Order 1920, as we discuss below. The critical path to BESS deployment relies on market signals that appropriately value the many benefits that BESS can provide as a grid asset.

In this issue, we examine the legal, regulatory, commercial, and technological dimensions of a storage market that is growing faster, and becoming more complex than ever before.

Energy Storage Blogs

The Prohibited Foreign Entity (or FEOC) Rules and Battery Storage

July 16, 2026 | By Aaron Lang

Over the past year, battery storage developers and equipment manufacturers have had to contend with new “Prohibited Foreign Entity” (PFE) rules—commonly called the FEOC (“foreign entity of concern”) requirements.

Enacted on July 4, 2025, as part of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA), the PFE rules bar developers and manufacturers with specified ties to certain foreign entities—primarily entities with certain ties to China—from eligibility for key federal tax credits—including the Section 48E clean energy investment tax credit (ITC), the Section 45Y clean energy production tax credit (PTC), and the Section 45X advanced manufacturing credit. This post analyzes the PFE rules specifically as they relate to the battery storage industry.

Read more here.

Virtual Power Plants: The Distributed Energy Revolution Has Arrived

July 14, 2026 | By Peter Ross

The electric grid is under extraordinary stress. Electricity demand is surging—driven in large part by the explosive growth of data centers, widespread electrification, and the proliferation of AI workloads—while the infrastructure needed to meet that demand is mired in historic delays. Gas turbines are backlogged through at least 2028. Over two terawatts of generation capacity languish in interconnection queues, where average timelines now exceed five years. Transformer wait times have doubled. In this environment, traditional approaches to grid expansion are simply not keeping pace.

Read more here.

Client Spotlight Interview: Alsym Energy

July 14, 2026 | By Mark Haddad

Our partner Mark Haddad recently sat down with Mukesh Chatter, the CEO of our client Alsym Energy, to discuss Alsym’s journey and the future of energy storage, including the benefits of sodium-ion batteries, Alsym’s physics-informed AI platform for product development, and advice for climate tech entrepreneurs.

Read more here.

Transmission Planning: The Unsung Use Case for Battery Storage

July 8, 2026 | By Rebecca Rogers

2025 was decidedly the Year of the Battery, and the trend of expanding and optimizing the plethora of applications for battery storage systems has continued this year. Given ever-shifting economic outcomes and market conditions, however, the ongoing challenge for battery storage may not be so much what to do with it but how to prioritize its use cases. Tax credits for battery storage dodged several bullets from the OBBBA that hit solar and wind, but given that the majority of battery components are still exposed to FEOC restrictions, monetizing those tax credits for utility-scale BESS will continue to require careful navigation. Major electric vehicle manufacturers pivoted in 2025 to producing grid-scale battery systems when EV tax credits were gutted by the OBBA, but soaring gas prices caused by, among other things, the war with Iran, reignited interest in EVs as a commonsense hedge for household and commercial transportation budgets.

Read more here.

Siting Battery Storage in Massachusetts: A New Regulatory Landscape

July 1, 2026 | By Aaron Lang, Zachary Gerson, Anjika Pai

Battery energy storage systems (“BESS”) are central to Massachusetts’ clean energy strategy. The Commonwealth has committed to procuring approximately 5,000 megawatts of energy storage by July 31, 2030, and procurements are ongoing. At the same time, the regulatory landscape for developing BESS is evolving in fundamental ways. Among the most significant reforms is the new consolidated siting and permitting framework for BESS and other clean energy projects set to begin on July 1, 2026.

Read more here.

Recent Blog Posts

PJM Takes a Step Forward in Dealing with Capacity Shortfall: Important FERC Filing Coming Soon

July 7, 2026 | By Zachary Gerson

It is a busy time for PJM. The Regional Transmission Organization, which coordinates wholesale electricity markets in 13 states and the District of Columbia, serving over 67 million people, has emerged as patient zero for fears that rapidly expanding demand—spurred by newly surging data center proposals and longstanding struggles to connect new generation resources—could spike consumer costs and threaten reliability. But PJM and its stakeholders have been busy working to find solutions, taking an important step on June 30.

First, some background. In December 2025, PJM announced its 2027/2028 capacity auction results. As explained in PJM’s Auction Report, that auction failed to procure resources sufficient to meet PJM’s reliability requirement—a 20% reserve margin—coming in 6,632 MW short.

Read more here.

SEC Proposes Full Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules

June 1, 2026 | By Ryan Rourke Reed, Stacie Aarestad, Dan Clevenger

The Commission’s May 2026 proposal to withdraw its landmark climate disclosure regime marks a decisive shift in federal ESG rulemaking—with significant strategic implications for public companies, investors, and legal counsel navigating a fragmented disclosure landscape.

The Securities and Exchange Commission on May 29, 2026 issued a proposed rulemaking to rescind, in their entirety, the climate-related disclosure rules it adopted in March 2024. The proposed rules represent the culmination of more than two years of legal uncertainty surrounding the rules, which were stayed shortly after adoption, challenged in consolidated litigation before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, and ultimately abandoned by the Commission when it voted to withdraw its defense in March 2025. The proposal is now open for a 60-day public comment period.

Read more here.

What Regulators Can't See: The American Efficient Case and the Future of Demand-Side Oversight

May 28, 2026 | By Noah C. Shaw, Mack Ramsden, Anjika Pai

On April 15, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) imposed a $722 million civil penalty against American Efficient, LLC (“American Efficient”) and its affiliates in one of the largest enforcement actions in FERC’s history. Over more than a decade, the company collected roughly half a billion dollars in capacity market payments from PJM and MISO by claiming credit for energy efficiency resources that, according to FERC, it neither owned, controlled, nor caused to exist.

The case exposes fundamental gaps in how wholesale electricity markets verify demand-side resources, particularly energy efficiency.

Read more here.

EPA Proposes to Revisit PFAS Drinking Water Rules

May 18, 2026 | By Seth D. Jaffe, Kevin Y. Chen

On May 18, 2026, EPA proposed two significant changes to the federal drinking water regulations for PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances), commonly known as “forever chemicals.” One would rescind the Biden-era standards for four categories of PFAS, and the other would extend the time for qualifying water systems to comply with existing standards for PFOA and PFOS by up to two additional years. Both proposals carry significant implications for regulated entities and environmental liabilities, yet both also face likely legal challenges—underscoring that the PFAS regulatory landscape continues to remain unsettled.

Read more here.

The 9th Circuit Affirms Dismissal in G.B. v. EPA; Is It the End (for now) For Citizens' Climate Litigation?

April 30, 2026 | By Seth D. Jaffe

Earlier this month, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed dismissal of plaintiffs’ claims in G.B. v. EPA, another of the children’s climate cases. The claims in G.B. differed from those recently dismissed in Juliana v. United States. As the opinion in G.B. noted, the plaintiffs in Juliana:

“Challenged federal policy far more sweeping in scale, including the Government’s decades-long practices of permitting, authorizing, and subsidizing fossil fuel extraction, development, consumption, and exportation, thus causing “atmospheric CO2 concentrations to escalate to levels unprecedented in human history.”

The complaint in G.B., on the other hand, was much more focused. The claims in G.B. centered on the government’s decision in cost-benefit analyses, including analyses of the social cost of carbon, to discount the value of future costs and benefits.

Read more here.

New York Senate Passes ASAP Act to Increase Solar Funding and Reduce Deployment Costs

April 29, 2026 | By Noah C. Shaw, Peter Ross, Elza Bouhassira

On April 21, 2026, the New York State Senate passed the Accelerate Solar for Affordable Power (ASAP) Act (2025-S6570A). The bill sets a new goal of 20 gigawatts (GW) of distributed solar energy capacity by 2035 and extends the NY-Sun program to facilitate reaching that goal. It also directs the New York Public Service Commission (PSC) to advance reforms to reduce the time and cost of interconnecting distributed energy resources (DERs), like solar and energy storage projects, to the grid.

If passed by the New York Assembly and signed by the Governor, the Act would be effective immediately upon its adoption.

Read more here.

Maine PUC Votes to Reopen Bid Window for Northern Maine Renewable Energy Generation & Transmission RFP

April 28th, 2026 | By Joshua Rosen

On April 28, 2026, the Maine Public Utilities Commission (the “Commission”) voted unanimously during its public deliberations session to reopen the bid window and issue an amended Request for Proposals (“RFP”) for Renewable Energy Generation and Transmission Projects under the Northern Maine Renewable Energy Development Program. Commissioner Bartlett proposed the action, framing it as an effort to increase the likelihood that the RFP will solicit proposals that are ratepayer-beneficial and result in the approval of contracts that are in the public interest. Commissioners Scully and Gilbert expressed agreement with the proposal. Commission staff are expected to issue an order reflecting this decision in the near term.

Read more here.

Court Annuls New York's Wetlands Regulations for Failure to Comply with SEQRA

April 14, 2026 | By Noah C. Shaw, Sarah Main, Elza Bouhassira

On April 8, 2026, Albany County Supreme Court Justice Richard M. Platkin made a splash when he annulled 6 NYCRR Part 664—New York State’s wetlands permitting regulations promulgated under the 2022 adoption of amendments to New York State Environmental Conservation Law Article 24, the Freshwater Wetlands Act—in its entirety for noncompliance with the State Environmental Quality Review Act (“SEQRA”). In October 2025, we discussed the wave of activity surrounding those regulations.

Read more here.

Massachusetts Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (CPACE): A New Era on the Horizon?

April 9, 2026 | By Jeffrey B. Mullan, Noah C. Shaw, Joshua Rosen

Nearly a decade ago, Massachusetts joined many other states in authorizing a Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (CPACE) program called PACE Massachusetts to support energy efficiency and renewable energy investments in commercial real estate. While the program has seen relatively limited uptake since its inception, legislative changes proposed in Governor Healey’s FY27 budget are poised to significantly broaden the program’s appeal and utility by removing the statutory savings-to-investment (“SIR”) requirement for CPACE-funded improvements. In this post we provide a comprehensive overview of the program’s structure, eligibility requirements, financing mechanics, and how the Governor’s proposal may open the floodgates for a significant uptick in CPACE market activity.

Read more here.

What We Are Reading

US Energy Storage Installations Hit Q1 Record, Up 32% Year Over Year: SEIA

May 26, 2026 | By Utility Dive

The United States added 9.7 GWh of battery storage in the first quarter of 2026, up 32% from last year. Utility-scale projects led the market, while business and home systems also grew. SEIA expects U.S. storage deployment to reach 613 GWh by 2030. Data centers are driving demand because batteries can support grid connection, backup power, and power quality. State storage targets support growth, but federal permitting delays may slow solar and storage projects.

Read more here.

Energy Storage Enters the 100-Gigawatt Era: Three Things to Know

May 7, 2026 | By BloombergNEF

Energy storage reached a new high in 2025, with 112 gigawatts added worldwide, up 48% from 2024. China led the market with more than half of all new storage, while the United States accounted for 16% of additions. BloombergNEF expects growth to continue, with annual additions projected to reach 158 gigawatts in 2026 and more than 300 gigawatts by 2036. This growth reflects falling costs, more renewable power on the grid, and rising demand from data centers, EV charging, and other power needs.

Conflict has had limited direct impact on storage markets so far, but higher fuel and power prices could increase demand for batteries in some regions. Lithium iron phosphate batteries still dominate the sector, but that mix may begin to change. Long-duration storage and sodium-ion batteries are gaining ground as policy support, supply deals, and cost cuts expand.

Read more here.

Why Solid-State Batteries Keep Short-Circuiting

March 25, 2026 | By MIT News

MIT researchers have identified a new explanation for dendrite formation, a key failure mechanism that has limited the development of solid-state batteries. These batteries could be safer and more energy-dense than conventional lithium-ion batteries, with potential applications in electric vehicles, consumer electronics, and grid-scale energy storage. Contrary to prior assumptions that dendrites primarily result from mechanical stress, the study found that high electrical currents can trigger chemical reactions that weaken the solid electrolyte and make it more vulnerable to cracking.

The findings suggest that simply making electrolytes stronger may not be enough; researchers may need to prioritize materials that are more chemically stable when exposed to lithium metal. For climate and energy stakeholders, the research could help accelerate next-generation battery technologies that support electrification and the broader clean-energy transition.

authors: Herb Weisbaum, The ConsumerMan, Herb Weisbaum, The ConsumerMan

text:
Buying an electric vehicle (EV) is one of the best ways to shield yourself from high gasoline prices. But new EVs still cost significantly more than comparable gas-powered or hybrid vehicles.

In May, the average transaction price for all new vehicles was $49,015, while the average new EV sold for $54,532, according to Cox Automotive.

Buying a used EV may be an affordable alternative. Because new electrics tend to lose value even faster than conventional cars, used EVs are often bargains.

The average used EV listed for sale in May cost $37,083, according to Cox Automotive—almost $17,500 less than the average price of a new electric vehicle.

That’s still roughly $2,200 more than the average used gas-powered vehicle, but since there’s no gas to buy, the payback period for the higher purchase price can be a year or less, depending on how much you drive.

According to the U.S. Department of Energy, switching from a gas-powered vehicle to an EV could save the owner up to $2,200 per year in fuel costs. (This figure was calculated in 2024, when the average price for a gallon of regular gasoline was $3.30, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.) DOE has a Vehicle Cost Calculator on its website to help you estimate potential savings for your situation.

An EV should also cost less to own because it requires less scheduled maintenance than a gas-powered vehicle. No tune-ups. No oil changes.

No exhaust repairs. And because they use regenerative braking, the brake systems last longer than those on conventional vehicles.

What About Supply?

The supply of used EVs for sale is increasing each month as leased models are returned to dealerships, which could help stabilize or drive down prices. It also means a wider selection of low-mileage models to choose from.

“If you want to get in [on electric technology], but you don’t want to tie up too much money, looking at a nearly new, particularly off-lease EV, may be the way to go right now,” said Paul Eisenstein, publisher of Headlight.News.

Consider Reliability

Although compared to gas-powered rides, EVs have fewer moving parts and require less maintenance, electric vehicles rely more heavily on software, digital displays, and electronic controls.

The added complexity of this advanced technology means many models suffer from reliability problems.

“EV reliability isn’t on par with gas cars or hybrids,” Consumer Reports cautions, especially for models 10 years or older. Based on CR’s annual reliability survey, EVs have about 80 percent more problems on average than gas-only cars and are less reliable than hybrids. CR members report problems with electric drive motors, charging, and batteries.

“Many of the problems with EVs and plug-in hybrids are because they are newer designs compared to gas technology, so some kinks still continue to be worked out,” said Jake Fisher, senior director of auto testing at Consumer Reports. “By comparison, hybrids have been around for nearly three decades, and the technology is tried and true.”

What About the Battery?

Carmakers are required to provide a battery warranty of eight years or 100,000 miles, which Kelly Blue Book notes is longer than most manufacturers’ powertrain warranties. And these warranties are transferable to the next owner.

Some automakers offer even longer battery coverage: Genesis, Hyundai, and Kia back their EV batteries with 10-year/100,000-mile warranties. Tesla provides eight-year battery coverage on all its models, but the battery packs on the Model S and Model X are covered for up to 150,000 miles, while those on the Model 3 and Model Y are covered for up to 120,000 miles.

“So, if you’re purchasing a used EV and you’re worried about the battery, which is kind of the most expensive thing to go wrong, you’re covered by a warranty for a long time,” said Keith Barry, Consumer Reports' senior auto reporter. “[That] might help you sleep at night if you purchase one of these cars.”

Except for two recent recalls (in which defective battery packs in Chevrolet Bolts and Hyundai Kona EVs were replaced by the manufacturer for free), an analysis of more than 30,000 car owners’ data by Recurrent, a company that helps value used EVs, finds that “battery replacements are exceedingly rare.”

Looking at all years and models of electrics, excluding those two recalls, data from Recurrent show that less than four percent of all battery packs have been replaced, including cars 10 years old or older. For EVs manufactured from 2022 onward, the replacement rate is only three-tenths of a percent.

Checkbook recommends having any used vehicle inspected by an independent mechanic before purchasing it. With an EV, ask the mechanic to check the battery to determine how much it’s degraded and its ability to hold a full charge.

It’s also a good idea to make sure the EV you’re considering has the latest software updates.

Where to Charge It?

It’s cheaper to charge at home than at a public charger, even in states with high electricity rates. A typical home EV charging system costs between $800 and $2,500 for both the equipment and standard installation.

Check whether your state, local government, or electric company offers rebates for home chargers. Some utilities offer special rates for time-of-day usage (you can save a lot by charging overnight) or discount rates for connecting to a home EV charger.

If you can’t have a charger at home and need to rely on public fast-charging stations, you may be better off buying a hybrid.

The Bottom Line

There are many advantages to buying a used EV, including a lower purchase price and operating costs, but you need to consider whether it makes sense for how and where you drive.

“It’s not just efficiency; EVs can be more rewarding to drive,” Voelk told Checkbook. “Heavy floor-mounted batteries give them a low center of gravity, giving them a sports car-like dynamic when slinging around corners. Plus, electric motors run smoother and quieter than internal combustion engines, with more satisfying power off the line.”

Speaking at ASSOCHAM's EV Ancillaries and Auto Components Conclave 2026, Sanjeev Chawla, additional development commissioner, MSME DFO, Karnal, said EV penetration in India currently stands at around 8.5%, or nearly 50 lakh vehicles, and is expected to reach 30% by 2030, creating significant opportunities for domestic component manufacturers.

GURGAON: Auto component manufacturers, particularly micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), need to reposition themselves to serve the electric vehicle (EV) ecosystem as India's EV market expands, government officials and industry experts said at an industry conclave in Gurugram on Friday. Speaking at ASSOCHAM's EV Ancillaries and Auto Components Conclave 2026, Sanjeev Chawla, additional development commissioner, MSME DFO, Karnal, said EV penetration in India currently stands at around 8.5%, or nearly 50 lakh vehicles, and is expected to reach 30% by 2030, creating significant opportunities for domestic component manufacturers. He urged MSMEs to explore opportunities across the EV value chain, including battery management systems, suspension systems, wiring harnesses, switches and brushless DC (BLDC) motors, while investing in innovation, intellectual property and patent filing to remain competitive. Chawla said long-term growth would depend on innovation, quality improvement through lean manufacturing and Industry 4.0 practices, and building an indigenous EV supply chain instead of relying on imports. Highlighting the technological shift, MK Sardana, coordinator, Department of Industries and Commerce, Haryana, said a conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle has around 2,000 moving parts compared to about 18 in an electric vehicle, underscoring the need for component manufacturers to diversify. He added that batteries account for nearly one-third of an EV's cost and that localisation of battery manufacturing should be a strategic priority. Sardana said Haryana's EV Policy, launched in 2022, will remain in force until 2027, while a dedicated MSME policy is expected within a month. He also highlighted the recently launched Invest in Haryana 2026 umbrella policy, under which electric mobility has been identified as a priority sector. Ajay Mohan Goyal, joint director, Department of Industries and Commerce, said Haryana accounts for nearly 50% of India's passenger car production and around 60% of motorcycle manufacturing, placing the state in a strong position to lead the EV transition. The conclave also focused on financing for MSMEs, localisation of EV components, export competitiveness, technology adoption, skilling and sustainable manufacturing, with experts saying the shift to electric mobility presents significant opportunities for India's traditional auto component industry.

text:
TRISO-X, the advanced nuclear fuel subsidiary of X-energy, has been awarded an $11 million grant by the State of Tennessee to support the expansion of its nuclear fuel manufacturing campus in Oak Ridge.

The funding, provided through Tennessee’s Nuclear Energy Supply Chain Investment Fund, is aimed at accelerating the development of advanced nuclear fuel production infrastructure and strengthening the domestic supply chain for next-generation nuclear reactors.

The investment also reinforces Tennessee’s growing role as a center for advanced nuclear technology and manufacturing.

Construction of second commercial-scale fuel fabrication facility

The grant will support the construction of a second commercial-scale fuel fabrication facility, known as TX-2, along with a dedicated research and development laboratory, TX-L. These new facilities will be built adjacent to TX-1, TRISO-X’s first commercial nuclear fuel fabrication plant, which is currently under construction in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. Together, the three facilities will create an integrated campus designed to manufacture advanced TRISO fuel while supporting research, innovation, and future production expansion.

“This is an important step in building a world-class nuclear fuel campus capable of powering next-generation nuclear,” said Joel Duling, President of TRISO-X. “Oak Ridge stands as a cornerstone of nuclear innovation, and we are proud to carry its legacy forward with the continued support of the State of Tennessee.”

One of world’s largest commercial-scale advanced nuclear fuel manufacturing centers

Once fully operational, the Oak Ridge campus is expected to become one of the world’s largest commercial-scale advanced nuclear fuel manufacturing centers. According to the company, the expanded facilities will have the capacity to produce enough TRISO fuel to support approximately 55 Xe-100 advanced small modular reactors, generating nearly 4.5 gigawatts of clean electricity. That amount of power would be sufficient to supply electricity to an estimated 3.3 million homes across the United States, highlighting the strategic importance of the project in meeting future energy demands.

The expansion is also expected to generate significant economic benefits for Tennessee. The project is projected to create more than 1,000 permanent, high-quality jobs while attracting additional investment to the state’s growing nuclear energy sector. State officials have described the initiative as an important step toward strengthening America’s advanced nuclear manufacturing capabilities and ensuring a secure domestic supply of nuclear fuel for emerging reactor technologies.

The announcement follows another major milestone for TRISO-X earlier this year, when the company received a 40-year Special Nuclear Material License from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The license authorizes commercial production of TRISO fuel using high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) and covers both the existing TX-1 facility and the planned TX-2 expansion. This regulatory approval positions the company to support the deployment of advanced reactors across the United States as demand for clean, reliable, and carbon-free energy continues to grow.

TRISO fuel is considered one of the most advanced nuclear fuel technologies currently available. Each fuel particle is encapsulated in multiple layers of ceramic and carbon materials, allowing it to withstand extremely high temperatures while enhancing safety and performance. These characteristics make TRISO fuel particularly well suited for advanced reactor designs that are expected to provide electricity, industrial heat, and energy for rapidly expanding sectors such as data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure.

With the support of the Tennessee government and the U.S. Department of Energy, the expansion of TRISO-X’s Oak Ridge campus marks a significant milestone in the development of the nation’s advanced nuclear energy ecosystem. By increasing domestic fuel production capacity and supporting next-generation reactor deployment, the project is expected to play an important role in strengthening U.S. energy security, promoting clean energy innovation, and reinforcing the country’s leadership in advanced nuclear technology.

text:
The concept of planetary coregulation bridges Earth system science and ecological philosophy. It describes how the Earth's major spheres—the atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, lithosphere, and biosphere—do not merely exist alongside one another, but actively and dynamically regulate each other's states.

Rather than a static, one-way chain of cause and effect, planetary coregulation represents a web of bidirectional feedback loops.

The Spheres of Planetary Coregulation

The self-regulating stability of the Holocene—the geological epoch that allowed human civilization to thrive—is the direct result of these deeply intertwined systems remaining within stable limits:

Atmosphere Biosphere: Plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, directly regulating the greenhouse effect, while atmospheric temperature and moisture determine the distribution and productivity of global biomes.

Ocean Atmosphere: The global conveyor belt (thermohaline circulation) redistributes heat across the planet, while the oceans absorb more than 90% of excess global heat and act as a massive carbon sink, directly coregulating atmospheric temperature and chemistry.

Lithosphere Atmosphere: Over geological timescales, tectonic activity, volcanic outgassing, and the weathering of silicate rocks act as a global thermostat, locking away or releasing carbon to keep the planet from permanently freezing or overheating.

Dysregulation and Planetary Boundaries

When human activities over-extract or heavily pollute these systems, we introduce "noise" that disrupts these coregulation loops, pushing the Earth into a state of planetary dysregulation.

The Planetary Boundaries framework, developed by scientists at the Stockholm Resilience Centre, identifies nine critical systems that regulate the Earth's stability:

Boundary/Process

Role in Coregulation

Transgression Status (as of 2026)

Climate Change

Regulates global heat retention and weather patterns.

Transgressed (Safe: <350 ppm; Current: ~423 ppm)

Biosphere Integrity

Maintains ecological resilience, genetic diversity, and nutrient recycling.

Transgressed

Biogeochemical Flows

Coregulates global nitrogen and phosphorus cycles.

Transgressed

Land-System Change

Determines forest cover, global moisture transport, and carbon absorption.

Transgressed

Freshwater Change

Crucial for global hydrological cycles (both ground and surface water).

Transgressed

Ocean Acidification

Marine chemistry coregulated by carbon absorption; directly impacts marine food webs.

Approaching Boundary

Coregulating with the Earth: The Human Connection

Beyond the cold biophysical data, there is a growing recognition of how human health—both physical and mental—is deeply intertwined with the regulation of our environment.

In psychology, co-regulation refers to how the nervous system of one individual can calm and stabilize the nervous system of another. Ecologically, many practices focus on environmental coregulation: the idea that spending intentional time in regulated, balanced natural environments (like ancient forests or quiet coastlines) allows the human nervous system to "borrow" that natural equilibrium, reducing stress and promoting physiological allostasis.

The Living Feedback Loop: We do not simply live on the Earth; we are an active variable within its coregulation matrix. Restoring global stability is not just about reducing emissions, but about actively participating in the mutual stewardship of the systems that keep us alive.

text:
On Thursday, a U.S. District Court Judge denied a Detroit manufacturing facility’s request to pause enforcement of a February court order requiring them to abide by the conditions of the Clean Air Act.

Earlier this year, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan ordered DTE Energy and three of its subsidiaries to pay a $100 million civil penalty, determining it had violated the Clean Air Act by failing to meet Clean Air Act standards at EES Coke Battery, located on Zug Island between Detroit and River Rouge.

DTE and EES Coke must also apply for new Clean Air Act permits, and pay an additional $20 million to fund a “Community Quality Action Committee” which would support local air quality improvement projects.

DTE is the operator for EES Coke, which produces metallurgical coke, a carbon-rich solid fuel used to make steel.

DTE and EES Coke appealed the decision to the U.S. Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals in March, and filed a request to stay requirements of the district court’s February order, including the provisions requiring them to establish the community quality action committee and obtain new permitting.

On Thursday, District Court Judge Gershwin Drain rejected that request, noting that allowing the stay to move forward would go against the commands of the Clean Air Act.

“Given the significant harm the Facility’s excess emissions have caused, and continue to cause, to the surrounding communities and the public at large, the public interest strongly favors denying the stay,” Drain wrote in his opinion.

Attorneys for the Sierra Club, which intervened in the case, cheered Drain’s decision.

“It’s very encouraging to see the Court stick to the relief that community members fought for and that they urgently need to breathe clean air,” Mary Rock, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, said in a statement. “DTE and EES Coke’s decision to pollute the community with illegal sulfur dioxide for more than a decade is unlawful, as the court correctly ruled in this case. During the trial, Detroit and River Rouge residents testified that they have trouble breathing and doing normal, everyday things like gardening and biking in their neighborhood. They deserve immediate justice from DTE and EES Coke.”

A DTE spokesperson said they were unable to comment, citing its pending litigation within the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals.

Today’s show is sponsored by the Electric Vehicle Association. Join up to support the electrification of transport today. And by CCAN Action Fund’s electric vehicle raffle for the planet. Buy your ticket today to support their mission to fight for cleaner air and a healthier environment, and get three chances to win a brand new EV with every ticket. And by EnergySage. Plan your own energy independence and insulate yourself from rising energy costs. And by you. Stick around to find out how to keep us 100% independent.

Welcome back to another episode of TEN, Transport Evolved News. Thanks for joining me. I hope you’re safe, well, and with someone you care about, who cares for you. I know the broader news headlines this week have been… well, rough at times. So here’s hoping the next thirty minutes help us feel a little safer, a little more, like we’re part of something.

Like last week, we’re starting today’s show with a little round-up of new Q2 and H1 figures from around the world. And there’s a lot to unpack. The Volkswagen Group published figures this week for the first half of the year, showing that demand for EVs across its brand lineup fell by 68.8% year-over-year in the U.S. and 47.9% in China, only rising in Europe by 8.4%. In its associated press release, it says its order books for EVs in Europe rose by 50% compared to year-end 2025, so it’s not all bad news. In the U.S., it enjoyed a resurgence in demand for the ID. Buzz just as its ID.4 goes on model-year hiatus. New data from Cox Automotive shows that EV sales in the U.S. during Q2 were the strongest they’ve been since President Trump canceled the federal tax incentive for EVs as the ongoing war in Iran hammers gas prices. BMW reported H1 EV declines overall globally year-over-year, but Q2 showed 5.2% growth driven by Neue Klasse launches in Europe, something it says it hopes to see continue as interest in its new models remains high. And there’s hope on the horizon. Chinese companies set a new export record of more than half a million plug-in vehicles during June, and global EV sales yet again hit two million, a figure not seen since late last year.

It’s been teased for several months, and this week, Volkswagen officially took the covers off its all-new ID. Cross electric crossover. A compact SUV built on the MEB+ platform, the ID. Cross is designed for the highly competitive compact car market. Standard tech includes connected Travel Assist, V2G capability and Plug and Charge, while the cabin mirrors the ID. Polo’s layout and design language. The ID. Cross offers three drivetrain options — 85 kilowatts, 99 kilowatts and 155 kilowatts — paired with 37 kilowatt-hour or 52 kilowatt-hour battery packs. The smaller battery pack option has DC charging support at up to 90 kilowatts, while the largest charges at 105 kilowatts. All models come standard with an 11-kilowatt bidirectional AC on-board charger. Not all pricing has been released, but in Germany the ID. Cross will start from just under 28,000 euro.

Mercedes-Benz unveiled its new AMG CLA 45 4MATIC+ this week. The most powerful all-electric CLA to date, the mid-size sedan promises some pretty bonkers performance. How bonkers? According to official specs, it does the stoplight sprint in under 2.7 seconds, thanks to a triple motor setup delivering a peak power output of 500 kW. That’s significantly more than the entry-level, non-AMG CLA, but this model isn’t just about fast sprint times — it’s also pretty efficient too, thanks to the same Axial Flux motors debuted in the Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door Coupé. At a peak charge rate of 330 kilowatts, the AMG CLA 45 4MATIC+ claims a WLTP range of 670 kilometers, 416 miles for the sedan, and 640 kilometers, 397 miles for the shooting brake. Pricing has yet to be released, but expect this one to be pretty pricey.

We love covering new personal electric transport on this channel, but if we want to kick fossil fuels to the curb, we need to transition public transit fleets to electric too. In the last few years, we’ve seen a real growth in the number of public bus fleets switching to electric, either by purchasing new or converting old buses to electric. The latter is a term called repowering. Many fleet operators have ignored it, but this week a new analysis from the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, aka EMPA, showed that opting for repowered buses over new electric ones could accelerate Europe’s transition to electric by fifteen years. At the heart of the analysis is the cost benefit of using existing fleet rolling stock with aftermarket conversion kits, lowering capital expenditure overall without slowing the electrification process. I’ll link to the study down below.

As some world governments, often backed by the auto industry, throw up roadblocks to a future where the sales of new internal combustion engine vehicles are banned, we’re starting to see more and more places announce and enact bans. This week, China’s Hainan Province became the first to implement a complete ban on new petrol-powered vehicles with a confirmed date of 2030. The island province’s geography, located off the southern coast of China’s mainland, makes it an ideal candidate for a full electric transition, as it will not only mean electrical generation can happen locally, but remove the need for shipping fossil fuels in from the mainland. Under the ban, set for 2030, which focuses on privately owned vehicles, new plug-in hybrids and range-extended EVs will be allowed to be sold. The province also plans to promote EV and hydrogen adoption for heavy-duty transport, cold-chain logistics and public transit.

Last year, Europe enacted import tariffs on Chinese EVs to protect European automakers from what it deemed anti-competitive subsidies. But as Transport & Environment shows in its latest analysis published this week, automakers have pivoted, shifting from importing fully-assembled vehicles to importing batteries from China and assembling cars locally, allowing both European and Chinese brands to dodge most tariffs. Meanwhile, T&E warns that as European automakers pressure lawmakers to ease CO2 targets, European brands are slowing their EV efforts while Chinese brands accelerate theirs. In short, even with EU protection, Western automakers can’t compete against more compelling Chinese models that are backed by deeper pockets for local European production.

The stock market reacted so violently to unsubstantiated rumors about the future of Lucid this week that it triggered an automatic stock market protection mechanism to temporarily hold trading twice. It began when a website posted a report alleging that restructuring firm AlixPartners — a company that Lucid is legitimately working with on corporate restructuring — had advised the Lucid board to consider strategic options including a take-private deal or Chapter 11 filing. With minimal sourcing and no market due diligence, traders panicked and the stock crashed over 50% intraday, triggering multiple volatility halts. Lucid quickly rebutted, stating AlixPartners had not recommended bankruptcy and is solely helping improve operational performance. The company has no special board committee exploring buyouts or restructuring, and most recent filings confirm sufficient liquidity to operate well into 2027. In normal times, these reports would attract federal scrutiny, but it’s not clear what, if anything, will happen now.

Despite earning some of the best sales figures during Q2 in the US for EVs, Toyota has officially delayed its production plans for the 2027 Toyota Highlander SUV. Its first all-electric three-row SUV was revealed in February and offers seating for up to seven in a two-three-two configuration or six in a two-two-two configuration. But as Cars.com reported this week, the model’s official production debut is being pushed into 2027 due to additional adjustments to the vehicle prior to launch. Meanwhile, the current ICE and hybrid Highlander variants will continue production through until December this year. The delay impacts not just Toyota, but also the Lexus TZ and Subaru Getaway, which are essentially rebadged Highlander EVs with specific tweaks for their respective marques. But such is the trend right now. As we were going to film this, we heard that the Honda Prologue has been cancelled in the US too. Yes, it’s too late to include it in this as a dedicated item, but I wanted to acknowledge it’s happened. We’ll cover it more next week.

As demand for power grows around the world, driven by a surge in data centers and AI, electricity grids are suffering after decades of underinvestment. In the US, that’s particularly apparent as the current president tries to avoid spending money earmarked by his predecessor for grid upgrades while simultaneously propping up unreliable and aging electricity generators and infrastructure. And new data, as collated by SolarTech_SD on Reddit this week, shows that so far this year, every US state has suffered a major power outage every month, with about 70% of those outages triggered by severe weather and 20% caused by aging infrastructure. The solution to this, aside from actually investing in the infrastructure, is for citizens and businesses to invest in micro-generation, redundant grid-tied battery systems and, of course, vehicle-to-grid. Here at the studio, I’ve experienced two small power cuts just this week. Due to weather from El Niño expected to deepen into the dog days of summer, this will get worse. Prepare now and make sure you’ve got additional resiliency to keep things running.

And to finish this segment, some depressing data from the US, as if that previous story wasn’t bad enough. It’s no secret that the Trump administration has worked hard to discourage and defund renewable energy and clean transportation since early last year. Now, a report by non-partisan business group E2 shows the cost. Since January 2025, 216 large-scale clean energy projects have been cancelled, closed or downsized. The damage is staggering. $90.8 billion in lost GDP during construction alone, $55 billion annually in foregone economic growth, $68.2 billion in cancelled private investment and $48.4 billion in lost annual operational spending. Construction wages of $53 billion and permanent jobs worth $31 billion have also vanished, along with anticipated tax revenues vanishing nearly $20 billion during construction and $12 billion a year annually. Add it all up and we have nearly 470,000 lost jobs and a renewable economy that’s left scarred. It’s going to take a very long time to reverse this poorly made decision process at the federal level and it will put the US behind on renewables for a generation or more.

Our recall reminders are coming next, but first I need to tell you about the EV Raffle for the Planet fundraiser from our non-profit friends at CCAN Action Fund, which is now just two weeks away from its July 30th prize draw. If you haven’t yet picked up your ticket for your chance to win one of three EV prizes, now’s the time to do it. Raffles like these are always popular, but the good news is that there are still thousands of tickets left for you to grab. Fewer tickets in the draw means your odds of winning are that much better, and with three EV prizes, those odds are pretty great. And those are your news shorts. There will be more next week.

Our final two stories are coming right up, but first a quick word of thanks. I mentioned in last week’s show, but at the start of June, my other half lost her job of 11 years to corporate restructuring, and I told you that I was worried about the channel’s future. But since then, we’ve seen an outpouring of support from all of you, both financial, emotional and more, keeping this channel afloat in a really difficult time. I don’t have enough words to express my gratitude, but we went from worrying about next month to feeling secure through until next year. My beloved is also getting interviews right now, so fingers crossed we’ll get some good news very soon. And while the crisis is over for now, we’d still love your support. Right now, TE is paying its usual bills, plus keeping a roof over my head, so if you’d like to help, please consider supporting us on Patreon, YouTube or by sending us donations at Ko-fi or through our mailing address. Sharing our content and engaging with us online also helps. And if you’re in the US and looking for a way to become more energy-independent, you can also support the show by using our long-time channel sponsor, EnergySage. It’s a great way to get trustworthy, verified solar experts, whether that’s for solar panels, getting a heat pump, or for those who rent, a community solar program membership. And it was EnergySage who I used many years ago when we put solar panels on the roof of our house. And wouldn’t you know it? Our panels are still churning out electrons every day, so it’s well worth it as the cost of utility-provided power keeps rising. However you support us, thank you. You really do rock, and we wouldn’t be here at all without you.

And now it’s time for our final two stories. It’s no secret that the world’s fossil fuel supply is feeling the pinch as the US war in Iran rumbles on, and we’re already seeing figures showing that more people are buying electric as a result. But that doesn’t mean that automakers and fuel companies are giving up on combustion engines. This week, Toyota Motor Europe, BMW Group, Bosch and Repsol announced a new six-month pilot program in Spain that will demonstrate, and I quote, “the real-world potential of vehicles running exclusively on renewable fuels.” What does that translate to? Well, liquid combustible fuels, renewable gasoline, which claims significant emission reductions compared to fossil fuels, though it’s still not zero carbon. Of course, it’s also worth noting that these fuels rely on combustion, generate emissions, and unlike EVs, require you to visit a filling station to fill up. I wonder why they’re so hell-bent on promoting this over EVs, eh?

And finally, one of the big stories that we’ve been tracking for the entirety of this year has been the global grid transition away from fossil fuels and towards renewable forms of electricity. And while there are some pretty big flies in the ointment of that transition, even though they’re having a minimal impact compared to all the gains, it’s always good to see renewables are absolutely spanking fossil fuel electricity when it comes to generation. And this week, we got a new one. In June, solar became the largest generator of electricity in the EU for only the third time on record, but it accounted for 25% of the bloc’s monthly power generation, a record 52 terawatt-hours. And while this peak is seasonal, driven by record summer heat and long daylight hours, it’s still very much worth celebrating. Even in the depth of winter, solar is now contributing 5% of the grid’s total power generation in Europe, and renewables are, en masse, growing and dominating other generation methods. The US president might be obsessed with coal, but the European Union has finally done what it should have done years ago. Kept it in the ground.

And if you are new to the channel, hi, please give us a sub, either on YouTube or wherever you saw this, which might have been PeerTube.

Finally, you matter. You’re important. And I am so very glad that you are here watching this show. I know the rest of the team are similarly grateful. I know that many people are struggling right now for a whole host of different reasons. And a month ago, that was me. I finish every week with this segment, because I want everyone to know that not only does it get better, but it’s important to hear the impact that you are making on the world. And I think it’s important to make sure that everyone does know what their impact is, especially at this point in history. The news headlines are scary, infuriating, and honestly, most of the time, it is now feeling like we are the ones in the mirror universe, but all hope is not lost because a cleaner, greener, safer, smarter and more equitable world has to be rooted in justice, fairness and a shared goal for all.
